But they, wanting to be light in themselves and not in the Lord, imagining the soul's nature to be what God is, are made into a thicker darkness by their dreadful arrogance, since they backed away even farther from you, the true Light that gives light to everyone coming into the world. Let them take heed what they say, and blush with shame; let them draw near to him and be enlightened, and their faces will not be ashamed. As for me — when I was deliberating about serving the Lord my God now, as I had long meant to, it was I who willed it, I who refused it; I, my own self. I neither willed it wholly nor refused it wholly. And so I was at war with myself, and torn apart by myself. And this tearing happened to me against my will, and yet it showed not the presence of some second mind but the punishment of my own. So it was no longer I who did it, but the sin that lived in me — the punishment of a sin more freely committed, in that I was a son of Adam.

For if there were as many contrary natures as there are conflicting wills, there would be not just two of them but many. Suppose someone is deliberating whether to go to their secret meeting or to the theater — these Manichees cry out, "Look, here are two natures: a good one drawing this way, a bad one dragging back the other!" For where else, they ask, does this hesitation between conflicting wills come from? But I say both wills are bad: the one that draws toward their meeting as much as the one that draws back to the theater. They cannot believe that the will which draws toward them might be anything but good. Well then — suppose one of us were deliberating, and amid the clash of two wills were torn over whether to go to the theater or to our church: would not these men too be torn over what to answer? For either they must admit — which they would hate to do — that the will drawing a man to our church is good, just as good as the will of those who have received their own mysteries and are held by them; or they must suppose two evil natures and two evil souls battling in one man, and then it will not be true, as they say, that one is good and the other bad; or they must be converted to the truth and stop denying that, when a person deliberates, it is one single soul tossing between contrary wills.

So let them stop saying, when they notice two conflicting wills in one man, that the conflict is between two contrary souls, of two contrary substances, from two contrary first principles, one good and one bad. For you, the true God, disprove them, check them, convict them — as when, both wills being bad, a man deliberates whether to kill someone by poison or by the sword; whether to grab this estate of another's or that one, when he cannot have both; whether to spend his money on pleasure or hoard it out of greed; whether to go to the circus or the theater, if both are open the same day; or, a third thing, to rob a house, given the chance; or, a fourth, to commit adultery, if the opportunity is there too — all of these falling together in the same span of time, all equally wanted, though they cannot all be done at once. For they tear the mind apart among four wills, or even more, given the vast variety of things a man can crave — and yet the Manichees do not claim there are that many different substances in us. The same holds for good wills. For I ask them: is it good to take pleasure in reading the Apostle? Is it good to take pleasure in a quiet Psalm? Is it good to discuss the Gospel? To each they will answer, "It is good." Well then — what if all of them give equal pleasure, and all at the same moment? Do not the different wills pull the mind apart while it deliberates which to choose? Yet all are good, and they are at odds until one is chosen, and the whole will, that was split into many, can move toward that one. So too, when eternity above delights us, and the pleasure of a passing good holds us down below, it is one and the same soul that does not will this or that with its whole will, and so is torn apart by heavy distress, since out of the truth it puts the one first, but out of habit it does not put the other aside.

So I was sick at heart and tormented, accusing myself far more bitterly than usual, twisting and turning in my chain until it should be wholly broken — the chain that now held me only by a thread, but held me still. And you, Lord, pressed hard on my inmost parts with a severe mercy, doubling the lashes of fear and shame, so that I would not give way again, and so that the last thin thread, not yet snapped, would not knit itself back together and bind me tighter than before. For I kept saying to myself, "Let it be done now, let it be done now." And as I spoke I was on the very edge of doing it — I all but did it, and did not; yet I did not slide back to my old state, but kept my footing close by, and caught my breath. And I tried again, and came a little nearer, and a little nearer still, and all but touched it, all but grasped it; and yet I did not reach it, did not touch or take hold, hanging back from dying to death and living to life — the worse, which I was used to, having more power over me than the better, which I was not. And the very instant in which I was to become something other than I was — the nearer it came, the greater the horror it struck into me; yet it did not strike me back, did not turn me away, but held me hanging there.

The trifles of trifles, the vanities of vanities, my old mistresses, still held me back; they plucked at the garment of my flesh and whispered softly, "Are you sending us away? From this moment, will we never be with you again, ever? From this moment, will this thing and that be forbidden you forever?" And what was it they were hinting at in what I have called "this and that" — what were they hinting at, my God? Let your mercy turn it away from the soul of your servant! What filth they hinted at, what disgraces! And now I was hearing them far less than half as loud; they no longer faced me openly to argue, but muttered, as it were, behind my back, and slyly tugged at me as I was leaving, to make me look back at them. Still they held me up, so that I hung back from tearing myself loose and shaking myself free of them and leaping over to where I was being called — while a violent habit kept saying to me, "Do you really think you can live without them?"

But now it spoke very faintly. For on that side toward which I had set my face, and which I trembled to cross to, there appeared to me the chaste dignity of Continence — serene, but not slack in her gladness, honorably coaxing me to come and not to hesitate, stretching out holy hands to take me in and embrace me, hands full of crowds of good examples. There were so many boys and girls there, a multitude of the young and of every age, grave widows and gray-haired virgins; and in all of them Continence herself, not barren but the fruitful mother of children of joy, by you, her Husband, O Lord. And she smiled at me with a coaxing mockery, as if to say: "Can you not do what these young men and these young women can? Or can any of them do it of themselves, and not rather in the Lord their God? The Lord their God gave me to them. Why do you stand on your own feet, and so not stand at all? Throw yourself on him; do not be afraid. He will not draw back and let you fall. Throw yourself on him without fear; he will catch you and heal you." And I blushed deep, for I still heard the muttering of those trifles, and hung there in suspense. And again she seemed to say, "Stop your ears against your unclean members on the earth, that they may be put to death. They tell you of delights — but not such delights as the law of the Lord your God." This whole quarrel in my heart was self against self alone. And Alypius, sitting close beside me, waited in silence for the outcome of my strange agitation.

But when a deep self-searching had dredged up out of the secret depths of my soul all my misery and heaped it before the eyes of my heart, a mighty storm broke, bringing a mighty downpour of tears. And to pour them out in full, with all their natural cries, I got up and left Alypius — solitude seemed fitter for the business of weeping — and went off far enough that even his presence would not weigh on me. So it was with me then, and he sensed it; for I suppose I had said something in which the sound of my voice was already thick with weeping, and so had risen. He stayed where we had been sitting, utterly amazed. I flung myself down — how, I do not know — under a certain fig tree, and let my tears run free; and the floods of my eyes broke out, an acceptable sacrifice to you. And I said much to you — not in these words, but to this effect: And you, Lord — how long? How long, Lord? Will you be angry forever? Do not remember our old wrongs against us. For I felt I was still held fast by them, and I sent up these grieving cries: How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not this very hour an end to my uncleanness?

So I was speaking, and weeping, in the bitterest contrition of my heart, when suddenly I heard a voice from a nearby house — a boy's voice, or a girl's, I do not know — chanting, and over and over repeating, "Take up and read, take up and read." At once my face changed, and I began to think hard whether children sang anything like this in any kind of game, and I could not remember ever having heard it. So I checked the flood of my tears and stood up, taking it to be nothing other than a command from God to open the book and read the first passage I came upon. For I had heard of Antony, that he had once come in during the reading of the Gospel and taken the words as if spoken to him: Go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. And by such an oracle he was at once converted to you. So I went back quickly to where Alypius was sitting, for there I had laid down the book of the Apostle when I got up. I snatched it, opened it, and read in silence the first passage my eyes fell on: Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in lust and wantonness, not in strife and envy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh and its cravings. I had no wish to read further, and no need. For instantly, as I came to the end of that sentence, it was as if a light of assurance had been poured into my heart, and all the dark of doubt scattered away.

Then, marking the place with my finger, or with something else, I closed the book, and with a calm face told Alypius. And he told me, in turn, what had been happening in him, which I had not known. He asked to see what I had read. I showed him; and he looked beyond what I had read, to what came next, which I had not seen. It was this: Receive the one who is weak in faith. He took it to himself, and told me. And by that word of counsel he was strengthened; and with a good resolve and purpose, fully in keeping with the character in which he had always — and far for the better — differed from me, he joined me, without any agitated delay. From there we go in to my mother. We tell her. She rejoices. We relate, in order, how it came about, and she leaps for joy and triumphs, and blesses you, who are able to do above all that we ask or imagine. For she saw that you had given her, in my case, far more than she had been used to begging for with her pitiful, grief-stricken groans. For you converted me to yourself, so that I sought neither a wife nor any hope of this world, but stood firm on that rule of faith where, so many years before, you had shown me to her in a vision. And you turned her mourning into a joy far richer than she had wished, and far dearer and purer than the joy she had once asked for in grandchildren of my body.
books.title: The Garden: Take Up and Read

books.label: Book IX
paragraphs: O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid. You have broken the chains that bound me; I will offer you the sacrifice of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise you; let all my bones say, O Lord, who is like you? Let them say it, and answer me, and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Who am I, and what am I? What evil has there not been, whether in my deeds, or, if not my deeds, then my words, or, if not my words, then my will? But you, Lord, are good and merciful; your right hand reached down into the depth of my death and from the bottom of my heart emptied out that pit of corruption. And the whole of your gift was this: that I should stop willing what I had willed, and begin to will what you willed. But where, through all those years, and out of what low and hidden recess, was my free will called forth in a single moment, so that I bent my neck to your easy yoke and my shoulders to your light burden, O Christ Jesus, my Helper and my Redeemer? How sweet it suddenly became to me to go without the sweetness of those trifles! What I had been afraid to lose, it was now a joy to let go. For you cast them out of me, you who are the true and highest sweetness; you cast them out, and in their place you entered in yourself, sweeter than every pleasure, though not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light, yet more hidden than every depth; higher than every honor, but not to those who are high in their own eyes. Now my soul was free from the gnawing cares of campaigning and getting, of wallowing in filth and scratching the itch of lust. And like a child I spoke freely to you, my brightness, my riches, my health, the Lord my God.

And I resolved, in your sight, not to tear myself loose all at once with a great noise, but quietly to withdraw the service of my tongue from the marketplace of hired speech, so that the young — students not of your law, not of your peace, but of lying fantasies and courtroom skirmishes — should no longer buy from my mouth the weapons for their madness. It fell out conveniently: there were only a few days left before the vintage holidays, and I decided to endure them, and then to take my leave in good order, since, having been bought by you, I would no longer put myself up for sale. So our plan was known to you, but among men it was known only to our own circle of friends. For we had agreed not to let it out to anyone else — though to us, now climbing up out of the valley of tears and singing the song of ascents, you had given sharp arrows and burning coals against the cunning tongue, the tongue that would block our way under the show of giving us good advice, and out of love would devour us, the way a man devours his food.

You had pierced our hearts with your love, and we carried your words fixed deep inside us; and the examples of your servants, whom you had turned from black to shining and from dead to living, were heaped up in the storehouse of our thoughts and set fire to our heavy sluggishness, so that we should not sink down into the abyss. They kindled us so fiercely that every gust from the cunning tongues of those who argued against us could only fan the flame the hotter, not put it out. And yet, because for the sake of your Name, which you have made holy throughout the earth, this vow and purpose of mine might also find people to praise it, it began to look like showing off — not to wait for the holiday now so near, but to quit ahead of time a public office that stood before everyone's eyes; so that everyone, watching what I did and noting how close the vintage was that I had wanted to anticipate, would have a great deal to say about me, as though I had wanted to be seen as someone important. And what would it have gained me, that people should pore over my motives and dispute about them, and that the good we were doing should be spoken of as evil?

There was something else, too, that had troubled me. That very summer, under the strain of too much literary work, my lungs had begun to fail; I breathed deeply only with difficulty, and the pain in my chest showed they were injured and refused me any full or lengthy speaking. This had troubled me, for it all but forced me, of necessity, to set down the burden of teaching, or at least, if I could be cured and recover, to set it aside for a while. But once the full longing for the quiet in which I might come to see that you are the Lord had risen in me and settled firm, then — my God, you know it — I began even to be glad that I had this second excuse, and a true one, not invented, which might somewhat soften the offense of those who, for their sons' sake, wished I would never have the freedom of your sons. So, full of that gladness, I held out until the stretch of time should run its course — some twenty days it may have been; yet they were borne with effort. The greed that used to help carry this heavy work had left me, and I was alone, and I would have been crushed, had not patience taken its place. Perhaps some of your servants, my brothers, will say I sinned in this, that with a heart fully set on serving you I let myself sit even one hour longer in the chair of lies. I will not argue the point. But have you not, O most merciful Lord, pardoned and forgiven this sin too, along with my other most horrible and deadly sins, in the holy water of baptism?

Verecundus was worn down with worry over this happiness of ours, for, held back by bonds that bound him most tightly, he saw that he would be cut off from us. He was not yet a Christian; his wife was one of the faithful, and it was she, more than any other chain, that fastened him and held him back from the journey we had now set out on. For he would not, he said, be a Christian on any terms but the one open to him, which was the one he could not take. Still, he kindly offered us the use of his country house for as long as we should stay there. You, Lord, will reward him in the resurrection of the just, for you have already given him the portion of the righteous. While we were away, now back in Rome, he fell sick in body, and in that sickness he was made a Christian and one of the faithful, and so departed this life. And you had mercy not only on him, but on us, lest, remembering the great kindness of our friend toward us and yet unable to count him among your flock, we should be torn apart by unbearable grief. Thanks be to you, our God; we are yours. Your hints and your comforts tell us so. Faithful to your promises, you now repay Verecundus for his country house at Cassiciacum — where, away from the fever of the world, we found our rest in you — with the everlasting freshness of your Paradise; for you have forgiven him his sins upon earth, on that rich mountain, the mountain that flows with milk, your own mountain.

He, then, was sorrowing at that time, but Nebridius was rejoicing. For although he too was not yet a Christian, and had fallen into the pit of that most poisonous error, believing the flesh of your Son to be a phantom, he had climbed out of it and come to believe as we did; and though he had not yet received any of the sacraments of your Church, he was a most ardent seeker after truth. Not long after our conversion and our rebirth in your baptism, when he too was a faithful member of the Catholic Church and was serving you in perfect chastity and self-control among his own people in Africa — his whole household having through him first been made Christian — you released him from the flesh, and now he lives in Abraham's bosom. Whatever that bosom may mean, there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, your child, O Lord, adopted now from a freedman. There he lives; for what other place could there be for such a soul? There he lives, in that place about which he used to ask me so many questions — me, a poor inexperienced man. Now he no longer lays his ear to my mouth, but lays the mouth of his spirit to your fountain, and drinks in as much wisdom as he can hold, as much as his thirst can take, endlessly happy. And I do not think he is so drunk on it that he forgets me; for you, Lord, whom he drinks, are mindful of us. So we were then, comforting Verecundus in his sorrow — as far as friendship allowed, given that our conversion had taken that turn — and urging him to be faithful within the bounds of his own condition, which was the married state; and we were waiting for Nebridius to follow us, which, being so near, he was all but ready to do. And so, at last, those days rolled by; long and many they seemed, for the love I bore to that easeful freedom in which I might sing to you from my inmost marrow: My heart has said to you, I have sought your face; your face, Lord, will I seek.

Now the day had come on which I was in fact to be set free from my professorship of rhetoric, the day from which, in my mind, I was already free. And it was done. You rescued my tongue, as you had already rescued my heart. And I blessed you, rejoicing, and retired with all my household to the villa. What I did there in writing — writing that was now enlisted in your service, though it still panted, in this breathing-space, with the fumes of the school of pride — my books bear witness: both what I argued out with others present, and what I argued with myself alone, before you; and what I set down for Nebridius, who was absent, my letters bear witness. And when will I have time enough to recount all your great kindnesses to us in those days, especially as I am hurrying on toward still greater mercies? For my memory calls me back, and it is sweet to me, O Lord, to confess to you by what inward goads you tamed me — how you leveled me, lowering the mountains and hills of my high imaginings, straightening my crookedness and smoothing my rough ways; and how you also subdued the brother of my heart, Alypius, to the name of your Only-Begotten, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a name he would not at first allow to be put into our writings. For he preferred them to taste of the lofty cedars of the schools, which the Lord has now broken down, rather than of the wholesome herbs of the Church, the antidote against serpents.

Oh, in what voices I spoke to you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, those faithful songs, those sounds of devotion that leave no room for a swelling spirit — still only a catechumen and a beginner in your true love, resting at that villa with Alypius, also a catechumen, and my mother holding fast to us, a woman in dress but with a man's faith, with the calm of her years, a mother's love, a Christian's devotion. Oh, what voices I sent up to you in those Psalms, and how they kindled me toward you and set me on fire to recite them, if I could, through the whole world, against the pride of the human race! And in fact they are sung through the whole world, and no one can hide himself from your heat. With what fierce and bitter sorrow I was angry at the Manichees! And then again I pitied them, for they did not know those sacraments, those medicines, and raged like madmen against the very cure that might have healed them of their madness. How I wished they could have been near me then, without my knowing they were there, that they might have watched my face and heard my words as I read the fourth Psalm in that time of my rest, and seen what that Psalm worked in me: When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in my distress you set me free. Have mercy on me, O Lord, and hear my prayer. I wish they could have heard what I said over those words, without my knowing whether they heard, so that they would not think I spoke it for their sake. For in truth I would not have said the same things, nor in the same way, if I had known they were listening and watching me; and even if I had said them, they would not have taken them in as I did when I spoke by myself and for myself, before you, out of the natural feeling of my soul.

I trembled with fear, and then again was kindled with hope and with joy in your mercy, O Father; and it all poured out through my eyes and my voice when your good Spirit, turning toward us, said: O you sons of men, how long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? For I had loved emptiness and chased after lies. And you, O Lord, had already glorified your Holy One, raising him from the dead and setting him at your right hand, from where, on high, he would send his promise, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. And he had already sent him, though I did not know it; he had sent him, because he was now glorified, risen from the dead and ascended into heaven. For until then the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. And the prophet cries out: How long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love emptiness and chase after lies? Know this, that the Lord has glorified his Holy One. He cries How long? He cries Know this. And I, for so long, not knowing, had loved emptiness and chased after lies; and so I heard, and trembled, because these words were spoken to the very kind of man I remembered I had been. For in those phantoms that I had held to be the truth, there was nothing but emptiness and lies; and I spoke many things aloud, earnestly and forcefully, in the bitterness of my remembering. I wish they could have heard it, those who still love emptiness and chase after lies! Perhaps they would have been shaken, and would have vomited it up, and you would have heard them when they cried out to you — for he who now intercedes with you for us died for us by a true death in the flesh.

I read on: Be angry, and sin not. And how I was moved, O my God, I who had now learned to be angry at myself for the things of the past, that I might not sin in the time to come! And rightly angry; for it was not some other nature, a people of darkness, that had sinned instead of me — as those say who are not angry at themselves, and so store up wrath against the day of wrath and of the revealing of your just judgment. Nor were my good things outside me any longer, nor sought with the eyes of flesh in that earthly sun. For those who would have their joy from outside themselves soon grow empty, and spill themselves out on the things that are seen and passing, and in their starving thoughts lick at the mere shadows of them. Oh, that they were worn out at last with their hunger, and would say, Who will show us any good? And we would answer, and they would hear: The light of your countenance is sealed upon us. For we are not that light which gives light to every man, but we are given light by you, so that, having once been darkness, we may be light in you. Oh, that they could see the eternal that is within, which, having tasted it, I grieved that I could not show them, so long as they brought me their heart in their eyes, which roved abroad away from you, while they said, Who will show us any good? For there, where I was angry within myself, in my own room, where I was inwardly pierced, where I had offered my sacrifice, killing my old self and beginning to plan a new life, putting my trust in you — there you had begun to grow sweet to me, and had put gladness in my heart. And I cried out as I read this on the page, finding it within. Nor would I be multiplied with worldly goods, wasting time and wasted by time, when I had, in your eternal and undivided Being, another corn and wine and oil.

And with a loud cry of my heart I cried out at the next verse: O, in peace! O, for the Selfsame! O, what did he say — I will lie down and sleep — for who shall stop us, when that saying comes to pass which is written, Death is swallowed up in victory? And you, surpassingly, are the Selfsame, who do not change; and in you is the rest that forgets all toil, for there is no one else with you, and we are not to seek the many other things that are not what you are. You alone, Lord, make me dwell in hope. I read, and I caught fire; and I could not find what to do with those who were deaf and dead, among whom I myself had been — a plague of a man, a bitter and a blind ranter against those writings that are made sweet with the honey of heaven and bright with your own light. And I was consumed with zeal against the enemies of this Scripture.

When shall I recall all that happened in those holy days? Yet I have not forgotten, nor will I pass over, the severity of your scourge and the wonderful swiftness of your mercy. You tormented me then with a pain in my teeth; and when it had grown so fierce that I could not speak, it came into my heart to ask all my friends who were present to pray for me to you, the God of every kind of health. I wrote this on wax and gave it to them to read. And the moment we had bowed our knees in humble devotion, the pain went away. But what pain it was! And how it went! I was frightened, O my Lord, my God; for from my infancy I had never known anything like it. And the power of your slightest nod sank deep into me, and rejoicing in faith I praised your Name — though that faith would not let me be at ease about my past sins, which were not yet forgiven me by your baptism.

When the vintage holidays were over, I gave notice to the people of Milan to find their students another seller of words, both because I had chosen to serve you, and because, with my difficulty in breathing and the pain in my chest, I was no longer fit for the work. And by letter I made known to your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and my present longings, asking his advice on which of your Scriptures I should best read to make myself readier and fitter to receive so great a grace. He recommended Isaiah the prophet — I believe because Isaiah, more clearly than the rest, foreshows the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles. But I did not understand the first passage of him, and, imagining the whole book to be like it, I laid it aside, to be taken up again when I was better practiced in the Lord's own words.

When the time came at last to give in my name for baptism, we left the country and returned to Milan. Alypius too was pleased to be reborn in you along with me, already clothed in the humility that befits your sacraments, and a most valiant tamer of his own body, so that he ventured, against all custom, to walk the frozen ground of Italy with his bare feet. And we took with us the boy Adeodatus, my son after the flesh, born of my sin. You had made him well. He was not yet fifteen, and in quickness of mind he outdid many grave and learned men. I confess to you your own gifts, O Lord my God, Maker of all things, and well able to reshape what is misshapen in us — for I had no part in that boy but the sin. That we brought him up in your discipline, it was you, no one else, who breathed it into us. I confess to you your gifts. There is a book of ours called The Teacher; it is a dialogue between him and me. You know that all the thoughts there put into the mouth of the one talking with me were his, in his sixteenth year. Much more, and still more remarkable, I found in him. That gift of his struck awe into me. And who but you could be the maker of such wonders? Soon you took his life from the earth, and now I remember him without anxiety, fearing nothing for his childhood or his youth or his whole self. We joined him to us, our companion in grace, to be brought up in your discipline; and we were baptized, and all anxiety about our past life fled from us. In those days I could not get my fill of the wondrous sweetness of pondering the depth of your design for the salvation of the human race. How I wept at your hymns and canticles, cut to the quick by the voices of your sweet-singing Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and the truth was distilled into my heart, and out of that the feeling of my devotion overflowed, and the tears ran down, and I was happy in them.

The Church of Milan had not long begun to practice this kind of comfort and encouragement, the brothers singing together with one accord of voice and heart. For it was about a year before, or not much more, that Justina, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, had persecuted your servant Ambrose on behalf of her heresy, into which the Arians had seduced her. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, bearing a leading part in those anxieties and vigils, lived for prayer. We ourselves, still not warmed through by the heat of your Spirit, were nonetheless stirred by the sight of the city, amazed and shaken. It was then that it was first set in place, after the manner of the Eastern churches, that hymns and psalms should be sung, so that the people should not grow faint under the weariness of their sorrow; and from that day to this the custom has been kept, and many — almost all — of your congregations in the other parts of the world have followed it.

It was then, too, that you revealed in a vision to that same bishop the place where the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius lay hidden, whom you had kept uncorrupted so many years in your secret treasury, so that you might bring them out at the right moment to check the fury of a woman — but an empress. For when they were found and dug up and carried with due honor to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were those healed who were tormented by unclean spirits, the demons themselves confessing it, but a certain man, a citizen well known to the city, who had been blind for many years, asked why the people were rejoicing in such confusion, and when he heard the reason, he sprang up and begged his guide to lead him there. Led there, he asked to be allowed to touch with his handkerchief the bier of your saints, whose death is precious in your sight. When he had done so, and put it to his eyes, they were opened at once. From there the news spread; from there your praises blazed and shone; from there the mind of that enemy, though not turned to the soundness of belief, was at least turned back from her fury of persecuting. Thanks be to you, O my God. From where, and to where, have you led my memory, that I should confess these things too to you — things which, great as they were, I had let slip in forgetfulness? And yet even then, when the fragrance of your ointments was so sweet, we did not run after you. And so I wept the more among the singing of your hymns, who had once only sighed after you, and was now at last breathing you in, so far as the breath can enter this house of ours that is made of grass.

You who make those of one mind dwell together in one house joined Euodius to us as well, a young man of our own city. While serving as an officer at court, he had been converted to you and baptized before us, and, laying down his worldly soldiering, he had girded himself for yours. We were together, and meant to live together in our devout purpose. We looked for the place where we might serve you most usefully, and together we were on our way back to Africa; and when we had come as far as Ostia, my mother departed this life. Much I leave out, for I am hurrying on. Receive my confessions and thanksgivings, O my God, for the countless things about which I keep silent. But I will not leave out whatever my soul would bring forth concerning your handmaid, who brought me forth — both in the flesh, that I might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, that I might be born into the light eternal. Not her gifts, but yours in her, would I speak of; for she did not make herself, nor did she rear herself. You created her; and neither her father nor her mother knew what kind of woman would come from them. It was the scepter of your Christ, the discipline of your only Son, in a Christian house, a sound member of your Church, that brought her up in the fear of you. And yet, for her good upbringing, she used to give the credit not so much to her mother's care as to that of a certain aged servant, who had carried her own father as a child on her back, the way little ones are often carried by older girls. For that reason, and for her great age and excellent character, she was well respected by the heads of that Christian household. And so the care of her master's daughters was entrusted to her, and she gave it diligent heed, holding them back firmly when she had to, with a holy strictness, and teaching them with a grave good sense. For except at the hours when they were fed, very temperately, at their parents' table, she would not let them drink even water, however parched with thirst they were, heading off a bad habit and adding this wholesome word: "You drink water now, because you have no power over the wine; but when you come to be married, and are made mistresses of the storerooms and cellars, you will look down on water, but the habit of drinking will hold." By this way of teaching, and the authority she had, she reined in the greediness of childhood and shaped their very thirst to such fine moderation that they no longer even wanted what they should not have.

And yet — as your handmaid told me, her son — a love of wine had crept up on her even so. For when, as the custom was, she was sent by her parents, like the sober girl she was, to draw wine from the cask, she would hold the cup under the open spout, and before pouring the wine into the flagon she would wet the tip of her lips with a little of it; for more than that her instinct refused. She did this not out of any craving for drink, but out of the overflow of youth, which bubbles up in playful little tricks that the gravity of their elders usually keeps down in young spirits. And so, by adding to that little drop a little more, day by day — for whoever despises small things falls little by little — she fell at last into the habit of greedily draining little cups almost brimful of wine. Where now was that wise old woman and her stern forbidding? Would anything have availed against a hidden disease, if your healing hand, O Lord, had not watched over us? Father, mother, and overseers absent, and you present — you who create, who call, who also through those set over us work something toward the saving of our souls — what did you do then, my God? How did you cure her? How did you heal her? Did you not draw out of another soul a hard and cutting taunt, like a surgeon's lancet from your secret store, and with a single stroke cut away all that rottenness? For a maidservant, with whom she used to go down to the cellar, quarreling one day, as servants do, with her little mistress when the two of them were alone, threw this fault in her face, with the most bitter insult, calling her a wine-bibber. Stung to the quick by that taunt, she saw the foulness of what she did, and at once condemned it and gave it up. As flattering friends pervert us, so spiteful enemies most often set us right. Yet you repay them not for what you accomplish through them, but for what they themselves intended. For that servant, in her anger, sought to wound her young mistress, not to mend her, and did it in private, either because the time and place of their quarrel happened to find them so, or for fear of getting into trouble herself for telling it so late. But you, Lord, Ruler of all things in heaven and on earth, who turn to your own purposes the deepest currents and the ordered turbulence of the flooding stream of time, by the very sickness of one soul healed another — so that no one who sees this should credit it to his own power, even when another, whom he wished to set right, is set right through some word of his.

Brought up in this modest and sober way, and made obedient to her parents more by you than by her parents to you, as soon as she was of marriageable age she was given to a husband, and served him as her lord. She worked hard to win him over to you, speaking of you to him by her way of life, by which you made her beautiful, and revered, and lovely, and admired by her husband. And she so bore his being unfaithful to her bed that she never had a quarrel with him over it; for she was waiting for your mercy upon him, that by believing in you he might be made chaste. And besides this, he was as hot in temper as he was warm in his affections. But she had learned not to stand up against an angry husband, not in deed only, but not even in word. Only when he had grown calm and quiet, and was in a state to take it, would she give him an account of what she had done, in case he had been too hasty in taking offense. And so, while many wives, who had gentler husbands, yet carried the marks of blows on their disfigured faces, and in friendly talk would blame their husbands' way of life, she would blame their tongues, giving them, as if in jest, this earnest advice: that from the moment they heard the marriage contract read out to them, they should think of it as the deed that made them servants, and so, remembering their station, should not set themselves up against their lords. And when they, knowing what a hot-tempered husband she put up with, were amazed that it had never been heard, nor shown by any sign, that Patricius had struck his wife, or that there had been so much as one day's quarrel between them, and asked her, in confidence, the reason, she taught them the practice I have described. Those who took it up found it good, and gave thanks; those who did not found no relief, and suffered.

Her mother-in-law, too, who at first had been set against her by the whispers of malicious servants, she so won over by attentiveness and steady endurance and meekness, that the older woman of her own accord disclosed to her son the meddling tongues that had disturbed the household peace between herself and her daughter-in-law, and asked him to put a stop to it. So, in obedience to his mother and for the good order of the house, he had those servants whipped, at the will of the one who had exposed them; and she promised the same reward to anyone who, to please her, should speak ill of her daughter-in-law. And after that no one dared, and they lived together with a remarkable sweetness of mutual kindness.

This great gift also you bestowed, O my God, my mercy, on that good handmaid of yours, in whose womb you created me: that wherever she could, between people at odds and out of all harmony, she showed herself such a peacemaker that, hearing on both sides the most bitter things — the kind that swollen and undigested anger spills out, when the rawness of enmity is breathed out in sour talk to a friend who is present, against an enemy who is not — she would never disclose anything from the one to the other except what might tend toward their reconciling. This might seem a small good to me, did I not know, to my grief, countless people who, through some horrible and far-spreading plague of sin, not only repeat to those already angry the things said in anger, but even add things that were never said at all; whereas, for human beings, it ought to seem a slight thing not to feed or fan ill will by ill words, unless one also takes pains, by good words, to quench it. Such was she — and you, her most inward Teacher, taught her in the school of the heart.

In the end she won even her own husband over to you, near the very close of his life on earth; nor did she have to complain of him, now that he was a believer, as she had borne with him before he believed. She was also the servant of your servants; whoever of them knew her praised and honored and loved you in her, for they felt your presence in her heart through the witness of a holy life and its fruits. For she had been the wife of one man, had repaid her parents, had governed her house piously, was well spoken of for good works; she had brought up her children, going into labor over them again and again, each time she saw them swerving away from you. And finally, of all of us your servants, O Lord — for by your own gift you let us speak — us, who before her falling asleep in you lived united together, having received the grace of your baptism, she cared for as though she had been the mother of us all, and served as though she had been the child of us all.

The day was now drawing near on which she was to depart this life — the day you knew well, though we did not — and it came about, by your secret arranging, as I believe, that she and I stood alone, leaning at a certain window that looked out onto the garden of the house where we were staying, at Ostia. There, far from the noise of the crowd, we were resting after the strain of a long journey, in readiness for the voyage. We were talking together, alone, very sweetly; and forgetting the things that were behind and reaching out to the things that were ahead, we asked each other, in the presence of the Truth, which is you, what the eternal life of the saints would be like — which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. And yet we panted with the mouth of our heart after those heavenly streams of your fountain, the fountain of life that is with you, that, sprinkled from it according to our small capacity, we might in some way turn our minds toward so great a mystery.

And when our talk had come to this — that the very highest delight of the bodily senses, in the very purest bodily light, set beside the sweetness of that life, was not worth comparing with it, or even worth mentioning — we lifted ourselves up with a more burning longing toward the Selfsame, and rose, step by step, through all bodily things, and through heaven itself, from which the sun and moon and stars shine down upon the earth. And still we climbed higher, in inward thought and speech and wonder at your works; and we came to our own minds, and went beyond them, to reach that region of never-failing plenty, where you feed Israel forever on the food of truth, and where life is the Wisdom by whom all these things are made, both what has been and what is to come — and she herself is not made, but is, as she has been, and so will be forever; or rather, in her there is no "has been" and no "will be," but only "is," for she is eternal, since to "have been" and to "be hereafter" are not eternal. And while we were speaking and panting after her, we touched her, a little, with one whole stroke of the heart; and we sighed, and left there, bound to her, the firstfruits of the Spirit, and came back down to the noise of our own mouths, where a word both begins and ends. And what is there like your Word, our Lord, who abides in himself without growing old, and makes all things new?

We were saying, then: If for anyone the tumult of the flesh fell silent; silent the images of earth and water and air; silent the heavens; and the soul itself fell silent, and passed beyond itself by no longer thinking of itself; silent all dreams and every imagined revelation, every tongue and every sign, and whatever comes to be only by passing away — for if anyone could listen, all these things say, We did not make ourselves; he made us who abides forever — if, having said this, they too should fall silent, having turned our ear toward him who made them, and he alone should speak, not through them but by himself, so that we might hear his Word, not through any tongue of flesh, nor an angel's voice, nor a clap of thunder, nor in the dark riddle of a likeness, but might hear his very Self, whom in all these things we love, hear him without them, as we two were just now straining toward him, and in a flash of thought touched that eternal Wisdom which abides over all — if this could be made to last, and all other visions of a far lower kind be withdrawn, and this one alone seize and absorb and enfold its beholder in these inward joys, so that life forever might be like that one moment of understanding for which we had just been sighing — would not this be: Enter into your Master's joy? And when will that be? When we shall all rise again, though we shall not all be changed?

Such things I was saying, and even if not in just this manner and these same words, yet you know, Lord, that on that day, while we were speaking of these things, and this world with all its delights was growing cheap to us as we spoke, my mother said: "Son, for my own part I no longer find any delight in anything in this life. What I am still to do here, and why I am here, I do not know, now that my hopes in this world are all fulfilled. There was one thing only for which I wished to linger a little while in this life: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has granted me this beyond my asking, for I see you now his servant, and despising even earthly happiness. What am I doing here?"

What I answered her to this, I do not remember. For scarcely five days later, or not much more, she fell ill of a fever. And one day in that sickness she fainted away and was for a while withdrawn from the things around her. We hurried to her; but she was soon brought back to her senses, and, looking at me and at my brother who stood by, she said to us, as though asking: "Where was I?" And then, looking steadily at us, stricken with grief, she said: "Here you will bury your mother." I kept silent and held back my tears; but my brother said something, wishing for her — as the happier lot — that she might die not in a strange land but in her own. At this she gave him an anxious look, checking him with her eyes for still tasting such things, and then, looking at me, she said: "See what he says"; and soon after, to us both: "Lay this body anywhere; let no care for it trouble you in the least. This one thing only I ask: that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you may be." And when she had spoken this thought in what words she could, she fell silent, struggling now with her worsening sickness.

But I, considering your gifts — you, the unseen God — which you pour into the hearts of your faithful ones, and from which wondrous fruits spring up, rejoiced and gave thanks to you, recalling what I had known before: how anxious and careful she had always been about her place of burial, which she had provided and made ready for herself beside the body of her husband. For because they had lived together in great harmony, she had wished also — so little can the human mind grasp the things of God — to add this to her happiness, and to have it remembered among men that, after her wandering across the seas, what was earthly of this united pair had been allowed to rest, united, beneath the same earth. When that empty wish had begun to fade from her heart through the fullness of your goodness, I did not know; and I rejoiced, marveling that she had disclosed herself to me in this way — though indeed in that talk of ours at the window too, when she said, "What am I doing here any longer?", she showed no desire to die in her own country. I heard afterward, as well, that while we were at Ostia she spoke one day, with a mother's openness, when I was not there, to some of my friends, about the contempt of this life and the blessing of death; and when they were amazed at such courage, which you had given to a woman, and asked whether she was not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city, she answered: "Nothing is far from God; nor need I fear that at the end of the world he will not know the place from which to raise me up." And so, on the ninth day of her sickness, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third of mine, that devout and holy soul was set free from the body.

I closed her eyes; and a vast sorrow welled up into my heart and was overflowing into tears, when at the same time, by the violent command of my mind, my eyes drank their own fountain dry again; and it went bitterly with me in that struggle. But when she breathed her last, the boy Adeodatus broke out in a loud wail; then, checked by all of us, he grew quiet. And in the same way a childish thing in me, that was finding its vent in weeping through the young voice of my heart, was checked and silenced. For we did not think it fitting to mark that funeral with tearful laments and groans, since by these people usually mourn the dead as though they were wretched, or wholly dead; but she was neither wretched in her death, nor at all dead. Of this we were sure, on good grounds — the witness of her good life and her unfeigned faith.

What, then, was it that hurt me so grievously within, but the fresh wound made by the sudden tearing-apart of that sweetest and dearest habit of living together? I rejoiced indeed in her testimony, when, in that last sickness, mingling her endearments with my dutiful care, she called me "dutiful," and said, with great affection, that she had never heard a single harsh or reproachful word come from my mouth against her. And yet, O my God, who made us, what comparison could there be between the honor I paid her and her servitude to me? Being then bereft of so great a comfort in her, my soul was wounded, and that life of ours was torn apart, the life that had been made one out of hers and mine together.

When the boy had been quieted from weeping, Euodius took up the Psalter and began to sing — our whole house answering him — the Psalm, I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment. And when they heard what we were doing, many of the brothers and the religious women gathered; and while those whose office it was made ready for the burial, as the custom is, I, in another part of the house where I might fittingly do so, talked with those who thought it not right to leave me alone, on a subject suited to the time; and with this balm of truth I eased the torment that you knew of, and they did not, as they listened intently, supposing that I was without any feeling of grief at all. But in your ears, where none of them could hear, I blamed the weakness of my feeling, and held back the flood of grief; and it gave way to me a little, but then came surging back like a tide — yet not so as to burst into tears, nor to change my face. Still I knew what I was holding down in my heart. And being very much displeased that these human things had such power over me, things that in the due order and appointment of our condition must of necessity come to pass, I grieved over my grief with a fresh grief, and so was worn down by a double sorrow.

And look — the body was carried out to burial, and we went and came back without tears. Not even in the prayers we poured out to you, when the Sacrifice of our ransom was offered for her, the body now set beside the grave before being laid in it, as the custom there is — not even during those prayers did I weep. Yet the whole day long I was secretly and heavily sad, and with a troubled mind I begged you, as best I could, to heal my sorrow; and you did not — impressing on my memory, I believe, by this one instance, how strong is the grip of every habit, even upon a soul that now feeds on no deceiving word. It seemed good to me, too, to go and bathe, having heard that the bath got its name — the Greek word for it — because it drives anxiety from the mind. And this also I confess to your mercy, Father of the fatherless: I bathed, and I was the same after as before. For the bitterness of my sorrow could not be sweated out of my heart. Then I slept, and woke again, and found my grief somewhat softened; and as I lay alone on my bed, I remembered those true verses of your Ambrose. For you are:

Maker of all, the Lord, and Ruler of the height, who, robing the day in light, have poured soft slumbers over the night, that to our limbs the power of toil may be renewed, and weary hearts be lifted that sink and cower, and sorrows be subdued.

And then, little by little, I came back to my old thoughts of your handmaid, her holy life toward you, her holy tenderness and attentiveness toward us, of which I was so suddenly deprived. And I longed to weep in your sight, for her and for myself, on her behalf and on my own. And I let go the tears I had been holding back, to flow as freely as they would, spreading them out as a bed for my heart, and on them it rested, for it was in your ears, not in those of men, who would have read my weeping with scorn. And now, Lord, in writing I confess it to you. Let him read it who will, and interpret it how he will; and if he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for one small fraction of an hour — the mother who for the time was dead to my eyes, who for so many years had wept for me that I might live in your eyes — let him not mock me, but rather, if he is a man of large charity, let him weep himself, for my sins, to you, the Father of all the brothers of your Christ.

But now, with a heart healed of that wound in which it might have seemed blameworthy for an earthly feeling, I pour out to you, our God, on behalf of that handmaid of yours, a far different kind of tears, flowing from a spirit shaken by the thought of the dangers that beset every soul that dies in Adam. For although she had been made alive in Christ even before she was released from the flesh, and had lived to the praise of your name in her faith and her conduct, yet I do not dare to say that from the time you reborn her in baptism, no word ever came from her mouth against your commandment. Your Son, the Truth, has said: Whoever shall say to his brother, You fool, shall be in danger of the fire of hell. And woe even to the praiseworthy life of men, if you should examine it with mercy laid aside! But because you are not strict to seek out our sins, we confidently hope to find some place with you. And whoever counts up his real merits to you, what is he counting up but your own gifts? Oh, that men would know themselves to be men, and that the one who boasts would boast in the Lord!

And so, O my Praise and my Life, God of my heart, laying aside for a while her good deeds, for which I give you thanks with joy, I now beg you for the sins of my mother. Hear me, I entreat you, through the Medicine of our wounds, who hung upon the tree, and who now, seated at your right hand, makes intercession to you for us. I know that she dealt mercifully, and from her heart forgave her debtors their debts; forgive her too her debts, whatever she may have run up in all those years since the water of salvation. Forgive her, Lord, forgive, I beg you; do not enter into judgment with her. Let your mercy be lifted high above your justice, since your words are true, and you have promised mercy to the merciful — whom you made to be merciful, you who will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion.

And I believe you have already done what I ask; but accept, O Lord, the free offerings of my mouth. For when the day of her dissolution was now at hand, she took no thought to have her body sumptuously wrapped, or embalmed with spices, nor did she long for a choice monument, or to be buried in her own land. None of this did she charge us with. She desired only that her name be remembered at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day, knowing that from it the holy Sacrifice is dispensed, by which the bond that stood against us is canceled — the Sacrifice through which the enemy was conquered, who, reckoning up our offenses and looking for something to charge us with, found nothing in him in whom we conquer. Who shall give him back the innocent blood? Who shall repay him the price with which he bought us, and so take us away from him? To the Sacrament of this our ransom your handmaid bound her soul by the bond of faith. Let no one tear her away from your protection; let neither the lion nor the dragon come between, by force or by craft. For she will not answer that she owes nothing, lest she be caught out and seized by the cunning accuser; but she will answer that her debts are forgiven her by him to whom no one can repay that price which he, who owed nothing, paid for us.

May she rest, then, in peace with her husband — before whom and after whom she had no other — whom she obeyed, with patience bringing forth fruit to you, that she might win him too for you. And inspire, O Lord my God, inspire your servants my brothers, your sons my masters, whom I serve with voice and heart and pen, that as many of them as read these confessions may remember at your altar Monica, your handmaid, together with Patricius, her husband of old, through whose bodies you brought me into this life, though how I do not know. May they remember with devout affection those who were my parents in this passing light, and my brothers under you, our Father, in our Catholic Mother, and my fellow citizens in that eternal Jerusalem for which your pilgrim people sighs from their setting out until their return. So shall my mother's last request of me be more abundantly fulfilled for her, through the prayers of many, by means of my confessions even more than by my prayers.
books.title: Monica's Death

books.label: Book X
paragraphs: Let me know you, O Lord, you who know me; let me know you, as I am known. Power of my soul, enter into it, and fit it to yourself, that you may have it and hold it without spot or wrinkle. This is my hope, and so I speak; and in this hope I rejoice, whenever I rejoice as I should. As for the other things of this life, the more we grieve over them, the less they deserve our grief; and the less we grieve, the more they deserve it. For look, you love the truth, and whoever does the truth comes into the light. This I would do, in my heart, before you, in confession; and in my writing, before many witnesses.

And from you, O Lord, to whose eyes the depths of a man's conscience lie bare, what could be hidden in me, even if I refused to confess it? I would be hiding you from myself, not myself from you. But now, since my groaning bears witness that I am displeased with myself, you shine out, and are pleasing, and beloved, and longed for, so that I am ashamed of myself, and turn away from myself, and choose you, and please neither you nor myself except in you. To you, then, O Lord, I lie open, whatever I am; and with what gain I confess to you, I have already said. I do it not with the words and sounds of the body, but with the words of my soul and the cry of my thought, which your ear knows. For when I am evil, to confess to you is nothing but to be displeased with myself; and when I am good, it is nothing but to claim no credit for myself, since you, O Lord, bless the godly, but first you make him godly when he was ungodly. So my confession, O my God, is made in your sight silently, and not silently. In sound it is silent; in feeling it cries aloud. For I say nothing right to other people that you have not already heard from me, nor do you hear anything from me that you have not first said to me.

What, then, have I to do with other people, that they should hear my confessions, as if they could heal all my diseases — a race curious to pry into the lives of others, and slow to mend their own? Why do they want to hear from me what I am, when they will not hear from you what they themselves are? And when they hear about me from me, how do they know whether I tell the truth, since no one knows what is in a man but the spirit of the man that is in him? But if they were to hear from you about themselves, they could not say, "The Lord is lying." For what is it to hear from you about themselves but to know themselves? And who knows himself and says, "It is false," unless he himself is lying? But because love believes all things — among those at least whom it binds to itself and makes one — I too, O Lord, will so confess to you that other people may hear, people to whom I cannot prove that I confess the truth; yet they believe me, those whose ears love opens to me.

But you, my inmost Physician, make plain to me what good I may gain by doing this. For the confessions of my past sins — which you have forgiven and covered over, that you might make me blessed in you, changing my soul by faith and by your sacrament — when they are read and heard, they stir up the heart, so that it does not sleep in despair and say, "I cannot," but wakes in the love of your mercy and the sweetness of your grace, by which whoever is weak is made strong, once through that grace he has come to know his own weakness. And the good love to hear of the past evils of those who are now free of them — not because the evils are evils, but because they once were and now are no longer. With what gain, then, O Lord my God, to whom my conscience makes its confession daily, trusting more in the hope of your mercy than in its own innocence — with what gain, I ask, do I, by this book, confess to other people as well, in your presence, what I now am, not what I have been? That other gain I have seen and spoken of. But what I now am, at this very moment of confessing, many wish to know, whether they have known me or not, who have heard from me or about me; but their ear is not at my heart, where I am, whatever I am. They wish to hear me confess what I am within, where their eye and ear and understanding cannot reach. They wish it, ready to believe — but will they truly know? For love, by which they are good, tells them that in my confessions I am not lying, and that same love in them believes me.

But for what gain would they want to hear this? Do they wish to rejoice with me, when they hear how near, by your gift, I come to you, and to pray for me, when they hear how much I am held back by my own weight? To such people I will reveal myself. For it is no small gain, O Lord my God, that thanks should be given to you by many on our behalf, and that you should be entreated by many for us. Let the brotherly mind love in me what you teach it to love, and lament in me what you teach it to lament. Let it be a brotherly mind that does this, not a stranger's — not the mind of those alien children whose mouth speaks emptiness and whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood — but the brotherly mind that, when it approves of me, rejoices for me, and when it disapproves, is sorry for me; because whether it approves or disapproves, it loves me. To such I will reveal myself; they will breathe easier at my good deeds and sigh over my bad ones. My good deeds are your doing and your gifts; my bad ones are my offenses and your judgments. Let them breathe easier at the one and sigh over the other; and let hymns and weeping rise into your sight out of the hearts of my brothers, your censers. And you, O Lord, be pleased with the incense of your holy temple; have mercy on me according to your great mercy, for your own name's sake; and never forsaking what you have begun, complete what is unfinished in me.

This is the gain of confessing what I am, not only what I have been: to confess it not before you alone, in a hidden joy mixed with trembling and a hidden sorrow mixed with hope, but also in the ears of the believing children of men, sharers in my joy and partners in my mortality, my fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, those who have gone before and those who are to follow, companions on my road. These are your servants, my brothers, whom you have willed to be your sons, my masters, whom you command me to serve, if I would live with you and from you. But this word of yours would have been small, had it only commanded by speaking and not gone before by doing. This, then, I do in deed and in word; this I do under your wings — in too great a danger, were not my soul subdued to you under your wings, and my weakness known to you. I am a little one, but my Father lives forever, and my Guardian is enough for me. For he is the same who begot me and who defends me; and you yourself are all my good, you, the Almighty, who are with me before I am with you. To such people, then, whom you command me to serve, I will reveal not what I have been, but what I now am and what I still am. But neither do I pass judgment on myself. In this way, then, let me be heard.

For you, Lord, are the one who judges me; because, although no one knows the things of a man but the spirit of a man that is in him, yet there is something of a man that not even the spirit of the man that is in him knows. But you, Lord, know everything in him, you who made him. As for me, though in your sight I despise myself and reckon myself dust and ashes, yet I know something of you that I do not know of myself. Truly, now we see through a glass, darkly, not yet face to face. So as long as I am away from you, I am more present to myself than to you; and yet I know that you cannot suffer any harm, while I do not know which temptations I can resist and which I cannot. But there is hope, because you are faithful, you who will not let us be tempted beyond our strength, but with the temptation will also make a way of escape, that we may be able to bear it. I will confess, then, what I know of myself; I will confess also what I do not know of myself. For what I do know of myself, I know by your shining upon me; and what I do not know of myself, I do not know until my darkness is made like noonday before your face.

It is not with doubt, but with sure knowledge, that I love you, Lord. You struck my heart with your word, and I loved you. Heaven and earth too, and all that is in them — look, on every side they tell me to love you, and they never stop telling everyone, so that no one has any excuse. But, more deeply, you will have mercy on whom you will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom you have had compassion; otherwise heaven and earth speak your praises to deaf ears. But what do I love when I love you? Not the beauty of any body, nor the rhythm of passing time, nor the brightness of light, so dear to these eyes, nor the sweet melodies of every kind of song, nor the fragrance of flowers and ointments and spices, not manna and honey, not the limbs that the body delights to embrace. None of these do I love when I love my God. And yet there is a kind of light I love, and a kind of voice, and a fragrance, and a food, and an embrace, when I love my God — the light, the voice, the fragrance, the food, the embrace of my inner self, where there shines into my soul a light no space can hold, and there sounds what no time carries off, and there breathes a fragrance no wind scatters, and there is a taste that no eating lessens, and there clings a closeness that no fullness pulls apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

And what is this? I asked the earth, and it answered, "I am not he"; and everything in it confessed the same. I asked the sea and the deeps and the living, crawling things, and they answered, "We are not your God; look above us." I asked the gusting air, and the whole air with all that lives in it answered, "Anaximenes was wrong; I am not God." I asked the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars: "Neither are we," they said, "the God you are looking for." And I said to all these things that crowd at the gateways of my flesh: "You have told me about my God, that you are not he; tell me something about him." And they cried out with a great voice, "He made us." My questioning of them was simply my attending to them, and their beauty was their answer. And I turned to myself and said, "Who are you?" And I answered, "A man." And here, present to me, are body and soul, the one outside, the other within. Through which of these should I seek my God? I had already sought him in the body, from earth up to heaven, as far as I could send the rays of my eyes for messengers. But the inner part is the better, for to it, as ruler and judge, all the bodily messengers brought back the answers of heaven and earth and all that is in them, who said, "We are not God, but he made us." These things my inner self came to know through the service of the outer; I, the inner self, knew them, I, the mind, through the senses of my body. I asked the whole frame of the world about my God, and it answered me, "I am not he, but he made me."

Is not this beauty of bodies plain to everyone whose senses are sound? Then why does it not say the same to all? Animals great and small see it, but they cannot question it, because no reason is set over their senses to judge what the senses report. But human beings can question it, so that, by the things that are made, they may clearly perceive the invisible things of God — though by loving those made things they make themselves subject to them, and subjects cannot judge. Nor do these things answer those who question them unless those who question can judge. Yet they do not change their appearance, showing one face to a man who only looks and another to a man who looks and questions, so as to seem one thing to this one and another to that; appearing the same to both, they are mute to one and eloquent to the other — or rather, they speak to all, but only those understand who compare the voice received from outside with the truth within. For truth tells me, "Neither heaven nor earth nor any other body is your God." Their very nature says this to whoever sees them: "We are a mass; a mass is less in a part than in the whole." Now to you I speak, O my soul, for you are my better part, since you give life to the whole mass of my body, breathing life into it, which no body can give to another body. But your God is, even for you, the Life of your life.

What, then, do I love when I love my God? Who is he, high above the head of my soul? By my very soul I will climb up to him. I will pass beyond that power by which I am joined to my body and fill its whole frame with life. By that power I cannot find my God, for then the horse and the mule, which have no understanding, might find him too, since it is by the same power that even their bodies live. But there is another power, not only the one by which I give life, but the one by which I give feeling to my flesh, which the Lord has made for me, telling the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but the eye that through it I should see, the ear that through it I should hear, and to the other senses, each in its place and office, their own work, which, though they differ, I, the one mind, carry out through them all. I will pass beyond this power of mine too; for the horse and the mule have it as well, since they too perceive through the body.

I will pass, then, beyond this power of my nature as well, rising by stages toward him who made me. And I come to the fields and vast palaces of memory, where lie the treasures of countless images, carried in from things of every kind that the senses have met. There is stored too whatever else we think out by enlarging or shrinking or in any way altering the things our senses have reached, and whatever else has been entrusted and laid up there that forgetting has not yet swallowed and buried. When I go in there, I call for whatever I want to be brought out, and some things come at once; others have to be sought longer, hauled as it were out of some deeper hiding place; others come rushing out in crowds, and while I am wanting and looking for one thing, they leap forward as if to say, "Maybe it's me?" These I drive away with the hand of my heart from the face of my remembering, until what I want is uncovered and steps out of its hiding place into view. Other things come up readily, in unbroken order, just as they are called for, the ones in front making way for those behind, and as they make way they sink out of sight, ready to come again when I will. All this happens whenever I recite anything from memory.

There everything is kept apart and under its own heading, each having entered by its own doorway: light and all colors and shapes of bodies by the eyes; every kind of sound by the ears; all smells by the doorway of the nostrils; all tastes by the mouth; and by the feeling of the whole body, what is hard or soft, hot or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light, whether outside the body or within it. All these the great harbor of memory takes in, with its numberless secret and unspeakable folds and recesses, to be ready and brought out when needed, each entering by its own gate and there laid up. And yet the things themselves do not go in; only the images of the things perceived are there, ready for thought to recall. How those images are formed, who can say, though it is plain by which sense each was brought in and stored? For even while I sit in darkness and silence, I can bring out colors in my memory if I want, and tell black from white and any other shades I please; nor do sounds break in and disturb the image drawn in through my eyes, which I am going over, although they too are there, lying dormant, stored apart. For these too I call for, and at once they appear. And though my tongue is still and my throat silent, I can sing whatever I want; nor do those images of colors, which are nonetheless there, push in and interrupt when another store, the one that flowed in through the ears, is called for. So with the rest, heaped in and up by the other senses, which I recall at will. I tell the scent of lilies from violets, though I am smelling nothing; I prefer honey to sweet wine, smooth to rough, while at that moment I am neither tasting nor touching anything, but only remembering.

All this I do within, in that vast court of my memory. For there are present to me heaven, earth, sea, and whatever I can think of in them, besides what I have forgotten. There too I meet myself, and recall myself, and what I have done, and when and where, and with what feelings I did it. There is everything I remember, whether from my own experience or on the word of others. Out of the same store I myself draw out, and combine with the past, fresh and fresh likenesses of things I have experienced or, from what I have experienced, have believed; and from these in turn I work out future actions and events and hopes, and all of these I think over again, as if present. "I will do this or that," I say to myself, in that great chamber of my mind, stocked with the images of so many and such great things, "and this or that will follow." "O that this or that might be!" "God forbid this or that!" So I speak to myself, and when I speak, the images of everything I speak of are present, drawn from the same storehouse of memory; nor could I speak of any of them at all, if the images were missing.

Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, O my God, a vast and boundless inner room. Who has ever reached its bottom? Yet this is a power of my mind and belongs to my nature, and I myself cannot grasp all that I am. Then is the mind too narrow to hold itself? And where can that part be which it does not hold? Is it outside it, and not within? How, then, does it not hold itself? Enormous wonder rises in me at this; amazement seizes me. And people go off to marvel at the heights of mountains, the huge waves of the sea, the broad currents of rivers, the reach of the ocean, and the circling of the stars — and they pass themselves by, and do not marvel that, while I was speaking of all these things, I did not see them with my eyes, and yet could not have spoken of them unless I were inwardly seeing, in my memory, those mountains and waves and rivers and stars that I have seen, and that ocean which I take on trust, and seeing them with the same vast distances between them as if I were looking at them out in the world. Yet I did not draw them into myself by seeing them, when with my eyes I beheld them; they themselves are not within me, only their images. And I know by which sense of the body each was stamped on me.

And yet it is not only these that the unmeasured capacity of my memory holds. Here too is everything I have learned of the liberal arts and not yet forgotten, withdrawn as it were to some inner place that is no place; and it is not the images of these that I hold, but the things themselves. For what literature is, what the art of debate is, how many kinds of questions there are — whatever of this I know exists in my memory in such a way that I have not taken in an image and left out the thing.
