It is not as if a sound had echoed and passed away, leaving its print on the ear so that it could be recalled as though still sounding when it sounds no longer; nor as a smell, while it passes and vanishes into the air, stirs the sense of smell and from there sends an image of itself into the memory, which we renew by remembering; nor as food, which has no taste left in the belly and yet in a way still tastes in the memory; nor as anything the body perceives by touch and which the memory still pictures when it has been taken away from us. For these things are not carried into the memory; only their images are caught up, with wonderful swiftness, and stored as in marvelous compartments, and from there wonderfully brought out again by the act of remembering.

But now, when I hear that there are three kinds of question — whether a thing is, what it is, of what sort it is — I do hold the images of the sounds of which those words are made, and I know that those sounds passed with a noise through the air and now are gone. But the things themselves, which those sounds signify, I never reached with any bodily sense, nor ever perceived anywhere but in my mind; and yet it is not their images that I have stored in my memory, but the things themselves. How they got into me, let them say if they can; for I have gone over all the gateways of my flesh and cannot find by which they entered. For the eyes say, "If they had color, we reported them." The ears say, "If they made a sound, we gave word of them." The nostrils say, "If they had a smell, they passed by us." The taste says, "Unless they had a flavor, do not ask me." The touch says, "If it had no size, I did not handle it, and if I did not handle it, I gave no notice of it." From where, then, and how did these things enter my memory? I do not know how. For when I learned them, I did not trust another man's mind, but recognized them in my own; and approving them as true, I entrusted them to my mind, laying them up as if where I might bring them out when I wished. So they were in me even before I learned them, but they were not in my memory. Where, then? And why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, "So it is, it is true," unless they were already in the memory, but so pushed back and buried in its deeper recesses that, had not someone else's prompting drawn them out, I might never have been able to think of them at all?

And so we find that to learn these things — the ones whose images we do not drink in through the senses, but perceive within, in themselves, without images, as they are — is nothing but to gather up, by thinking, and by careful attention to set ready at hand, as it were, those things which the memory already held scattered and unsorted, so that, now placed where before they lay unknown, neglected, and dispersed, they readily come to a mind grown familiar with them. How many things of this kind my memory carries, things already found out and, as I said, set ready at hand, which we are said to have learned and come to know — and if for some short stretch of time I stop calling them to mind, they sink again and slip back into the deeper recesses, so that they must be thought out again from there, as if new, for they have no other home, and must be gathered together once more in order to be known. That is, they must be collected, as it were, out of their scattering; from which the word cogitation, thinking-together, comes. For cogo, to collect, and cogito, to re-collect, stand to each other as ago and agito, facio and factito. But the mind has claimed this word for itself, so that not whatever is collected anyhow, but only what is re-collected, that is, gathered together, in the mind, is properly said to be thought.

The memory also holds the countless reasonings and laws of numbers and measurements, none of which any bodily sense has stamped on it, since they have neither color nor sound nor taste nor smell nor touch. I have heard the sounds of the words by which they are named when we discuss them; but the sounds are one thing, the things another. For the sounds are different in Greek and in Latin, but the things are neither Greek nor Latin nor any other language. I have seen the lines drawn by architects, fine as a spider's thread; but those mathematical lines are still something else, they are not the images of the lines my bodily eye showed me; whoever recognizes them within himself, without thinking of any body at all, knows them. I have perceived too the numbers we count with in all the senses of my body; but the numbers by which we count are different, and are not the images of those, and therefore they truly are. Let the man who does not see them laugh at me for saying these things, and I will pity him, while he laughs at me.

All these things I remember, and I remember how I learned them. I have also heard, and I remember, many false objections raised against them; and though the objections are false, it is not false that I remember them, and I remember too that I have told the difference between those truths and the falsehoods raised against them. And I see that my present telling-apart of these things is one thing, and my remembering that I often told them apart, when I often thought about them, is another. So I remember both that I have often understood these things, and I store up in my memory what I now discern and understand, so that later I may remember that I understood it now. So I also remember that I have remembered; and if later I shall recall that I was able now to remember these things, it is by the power of memory that I shall recall it.

The same memory holds also the feelings of my mind — not in the same way the mind itself holds them when it feels them, but in a far different way, according to a power of its own. For without being glad I remember that I was once glad; and without sorrow I recall a past sorrow. That I once feared, I review without fear; and a past longing I call to mind without longing. Sometimes, on the contrary, I remember a past sorrow with gladness, and a past gladness with sorrow. As to the body, this is no marvel, for mind is one thing, body another. If, then, I remember a past pain of the body with gladness, that is no great wonder. But here, this very memory is itself the mind — for when we put something in another's charge, to be kept in memory, we say, "See that you keep it in mind," and when we forget, we say, "It did not come to mind," and "It slipped my mind," calling the memory itself the mind. This being so, how is it that when with gladness I remember a past sorrow, the mind has gladness and the memory has sorrow — the mind is glad because of the gladness in it, yet the memory is not sad because of the sadness in it? Does the memory perhaps not belong to the mind? Who would say so? The memory, then, is, as it were, the stomach of the mind, and gladness and sadness are like sweet and bitter food; when they are committed to the memory, they are passed, as it were, into the stomach, where they can be stored but not tasted. It is absurd to think these really alike, and yet they are not wholly unlike.

But look — out of my memory I bring it, when I say that there are four disturbances of the mind: desire, gladness, fear, sorrow; and whatever I can argue about them, dividing each into its kinds and defining it, I find in my memory what to say, and from there I bring it out. And yet I am not stirred by any of these disturbances when, by calling them to mind, I remember them; and before I recalled them and brought them back, they were there, and therefore could be brought from there by recollection. Perhaps, then, as food is brought up out of the stomach by chewing the cud, so these are brought up out of the memory by recollection. Why, then, does the one who argues about them, recollecting them in this way, not taste in the mouth of his musing the sweetness of gladness or the bitterness of sorrow? Is the comparison unlike here, because it is not alike in every way? For who would willingly speak of these things, if every time we named grief or fear we were forced to grieve or to fear? And yet we could not speak of them unless we found in our memory not only the sounds of their names, by images stamped in through the bodily senses, but also the notions of the very things themselves, which we never received through any gateway of the body, but which the mind itself, perceiving them by the experience of its own passions, entrusted to the memory — or which the memory of itself retained, without being given them.

But whether by images or not, who can readily say? I name a stone, I name the sun, while the things themselves are not present to my senses, but their images are present to my memory. I name a pain of the body, yet it is not present with me, since nothing aches; yet unless its image were present in my memory, I would not know what to say of it, nor in discussion tell pain from pleasure. I name bodily health; being sound in body, the thing itself is present with me; yet unless its image too were present in my memory, I could in no way recall what the sound of that name means; nor, when health were named, would the sick recognize what was said, unless that same image were held by the power of memory, although the thing itself were absent from the body. I name the numbers we count with; and not their images, but they themselves are present in my memory. I name the image of the sun, and that image is present in my memory; for I do not recall the image of its image, but the image itself, which is present to me as I call it to mind. I name memory, and I recognize what I name. And where do I recognize it but in the memory itself? Is the memory present to itself by an image of itself, and not by itself?

And what of this — when I name forgetting, and likewise recognize what I name? How would I recognize it, if I did not remember it? I mean not the sound of the name, but the thing it signifies; and if I had forgotten the thing, I could not recognize what that sound means. So when I remember memory, memory itself is present to itself through itself; but when I remember forgetting, both are present, memory by which I remember and forgetting which I remember. But what is forgetting but the loss of memory? Then how can it be present so that I remember it, when, if it is present, I cannot remember? But if we hold in memory what we remember, and if we could never, on hearing the name, recognize the thing it signifies unless we remembered forgetting, then forgetting is held by memory. So it is present, that we may not forget, and yet, being present, we forget. Are we to understand from this that forgetting, when we remember it, is present to the memory not through itself but through its image? For if it were present through itself, it would make us not remember, but forget. Who now can search this out? Who can grasp how it is?

Lord, I truly toil at this, and toil within myself; I have become to myself a hard ground that costs too much sweat. For we are not now exploring the regions of the sky, or measuring the distances of the stars, or weighing the balance of the earth. It is I myself who remember, I the mind. It is no great wonder if what I myself am not should be far from me. But what is nearer to me than I am to myself? And look — the power of my own memory I do not understand, though I cannot even name myself without it. For what shall I say, when it is clear to me that I remember forgetting? Shall I say that what I remember is not in my memory? Or shall I say that forgetting is in my memory for this very purpose, that I should not forget? Both are utterly absurd. What third way is there? How can I say that it is the image of forgetting that my memory holds, and not forgetting itself, when I remember it? How could I even say this, since, when the image of anything is stamped on the memory, the thing itself must first be present, so that its image can be stamped? For this is how I remember Carthage, this is how I remember all the places I have been, the faces of people I have seen, and the things reported to me by the other senses; this is how I remember the health and sickness of the body. For when these things were present, my memory received from them images, which, being present with me, I could look on and bring back in my mind, when I remembered them in their absence. If, then, forgetting is held in the memory through its image and not through itself, then plainly it was once present, so that its image could be taken. But when it was present, how did it write its image in the memory, since forgetting by its presence wipes out even what it finds already noted? And yet, in whatever way — though that way is past conceiving and explaining — I am sure that I remember even forgetting itself, by which whatever we remember is blotted out.

Great is the power of memory; it is something to be feared, O my God — a deep and boundless manifold; and this thing is the mind, and this I myself am. What, then, am I, O my God? What is my nature? A life varied and manifold and beyond all measure. Look — in the plains and caves and caverns of my memory, past counting and past number, full of countless kinds of things, present either by images, as all bodies are, or by themselves, as the arts are, or by certain notions or impressions, as the feelings of the mind, which the memory holds even when the mind does not feel them, since whatever is in the memory is also in the mind — over all these I range, I rush this way and that, and I dive in as far as I can, and there is no end. So great is the power of memory, so great the power of life in a man even while he is mortal. What, then, shall I do, O you my true life, my God? I will pass even beyond this power of mine that is called memory; I will pass beyond it, that I may reach toward you, O sweet Light. What do you say to me? See, I am climbing up through my mind toward you who dwell above me. I will pass beyond this power of mine that is called memory, longing to reach you where you may be reached, and to cling to you where one may cling to you. For even beasts and birds have memory; otherwise they could not find their way back to their dens and nests, nor do many other things they are used to; indeed, they could grow used to nothing except by memory. I will pass, then, beyond memory too, that I may reach him who has set me apart from the four-footed beasts and made me wiser than the birds of the air. I will pass beyond memory also — and where shall I find you, you who are truly good and the sure sweetness? And where shall I find you? If I find you outside my memory, then I do not hold you in my memory. And how shall I find you, if I do not remember you?

For the woman who had lost her coin and looked for it with a lamp would never have found it unless she had remembered it. For when it was found, how would she know it was the same one, unless she remembered it? I remember having looked for and found many a thing; and I know this from experience, that when I was looking for any of them and was asked, "Is this it? Is that it?" I went on saying, "No," until the very thing I was after was offered to me. And had I not remembered it — whatever it was — then even if it were offered to me, I would not find it, because I could not recognize it. And so it always is, when we look for and find anything lost. And yet, when something is lost by chance from sight but not from memory — any visible body, say — its image is still held within, and it is looked for until it is restored to sight; and when it is found, it is recognized by the image that is within. Nor do we say we have found what was lost unless we recognize it, nor can we recognize it unless we remember it. But this was lost to the eyes, while it was kept in the memory.

But what about when the memory itself loses something, as happens when we forget and try to recollect? Where in the end do we search, but in the memory itself? And there, if one thing is offered by chance instead of another, we reject it, until the thing we are after meets us; and when it does, we say, "This is it" — which we could not say unless we recognized it, nor recognize unless we remembered it. So clearly we had forgotten it. Or had it not wholly escaped us, but was the lost part being sought out by the part we still held — the memory feeling that it was not carrying along altogether all it used to, and, crippled as it were by the loss of part of its old habit, demanding back what it missed? For instance, if we see or think of someone we know, and, having forgotten his name, try to recover it, whatever else comes up will not attach itself, because it was not in the habit of being thought of along with him, and so is rejected, until that comes which the knowledge can rest on, fitting its accustomed object evenly. And from where does that present itself but from the memory itself? For even when we are reminded of it by someone else and recognize it, it comes from there. We do not accept it as something new, but on recollection we agree that what was named is right. But if it were utterly blotted out of the mind, we would not remember it even when reminded. For we have not yet wholly forgotten what we remember that we have forgotten. What we have wholly forgotten, then, though lost, we cannot even look for.

How, then, do I seek you, O Lord? For when I seek you, my God, I seek a happy life. I will seek you, that my soul may live. For my body lives by my soul, and my soul by you. How, then, do I seek a happy life, since I do not have it until I can say, where I ought to say it, "It is enough"? How do I seek it? By remembering, as though I had forgotten it but still remembered that I had forgotten it? Or by longing to learn it as something unknown, having either never known it, or so forgotten it that I do not even remember that I have forgotten? Is not a happy life what everyone wills, and no one at all wills against? Where did they come to know it, that they should so will it? Where did they see it, that they should so love it? Truly we have it somehow, but how, I do not know. There is even another way, in which, when a man has it, then he is happy; and there are those who are blessed in hope. These have it in a lesser kind than those who have it in fact; yet they are better off than those who are happy neither in fact nor in hope. And even these, if they did not have it in some way, would not so will to be happy — and that they do so will is most certain. They have come to know it, then, somehow, and so have it by some kind of knowledge, though what kind I do not know; and I am at a loss whether it is in the memory, which, if it is, would mean we were once happy — whether each of us separately, or in that man who first sinned, in whom we all died and from whom we are all born into misery. This I do not now ask; I ask only whether the happy life is in the memory. For we would not love it unless we knew it. We hear the word, and we all admit that we desire the thing; for it is not the mere sound that delights us. When a Greek hears it in Latin, he is not delighted, since he does not know what is said; but we Latins are delighted, as he too would be, if he heard it in Greek; because the thing itself is neither Greek nor Latin, and Greeks and Latins and people of every other tongue long for it so earnestly. It is known, then, to all; and if all could be asked with one voice, "Would you be happy?" they would answer without doubt that they would. And this could not be, unless the thing of which it is the name were held in their memory.

But is it so as one remembers Carthage who has seen it? No. For a happy life is not seen with the eye, since it is not a body. Do we remember it as we remember numbers, then? No. For whoever has these in his knowledge does not still try to attain them; but a happy life we have in our knowledge, and so we love it, and yet we still long to attain it, that we may be happy. Do we remember it as we remember eloquence, then? No. For although, on hearing this name too, some call the thing to mind who are not yet eloquent, and many who long to be — which shows that it is in their knowledge — yet these have observed by their bodily senses that others are eloquent, and have been delighted, and desire to be the same (though indeed they would not be delighted but for some inward knowledge of it, nor wish to be the same unless they were delighted). But a happy life we do not experience in others by any bodily sense. Do we remember it, then, as we remember gladness? Perhaps; for my gladness I remember even when I am sad, as I remember a happy life when I am unhappy; nor did I ever see, hear, smell, taste, or touch my gladness with any bodily sense, but I experienced it in my mind when I was glad, and the knowledge of it clung to my memory, so that I can recall it sometimes with disgust, sometimes with longing, depending on the things in which I remember myself to have been glad. For I have been steeped in a kind of gladness even by foul things, which now, recalling them, I detest and curse; and at other times in good and honorable things, which I recall with longing, although they are perhaps no longer present; and so with sadness I recall a former gladness.

Where, then, and when did I experience my happy life, that I should remember it, and love it, and long for it? And it is not I alone, or a few besides, but all of us who would gladly be happy; which, unless by some sure knowledge we knew it, we would not with so sure a will desire. But how is this — that if two men are asked whether they would go to war, one perhaps would answer that he would and the other that he would not, but if they were asked whether they would be happy, both would say at once, without any hesitation, that they would? And for no other reason would the one go to war and the other not, than to be happy. Is it perhaps that, as one looks for his gladness in one thing, another in another, all agree in their desire to be happy, just as they would agree, if asked, that they wished to have gladness — and this gladness they call a happy life? So although one reaches this gladness by one means, another by another, all have one end they strive to reach, namely gladness. And since this is a thing that all must say they have experienced, it is therefore found in the memory, and recognized whenever the name of a happy life is spoken.

Far be it, Lord, far be it from the heart of your servant who here confesses to you — far be it that, whatever the gladness, I should think myself happy on its account. For there is a gladness not given to the ungodly, but to those who love you for your own sake, whose gladness is you yourself. And this is the happy life: to rejoice in you, of you, for you; this it is, and there is no other. For those who think there is another are chasing some other gladness, and not the true one; and yet their will is not turned wholly away from some likeness of gladness.

It is not certain, then, that all wish to be happy, since those who do not wish to rejoice in you, which alone is the happy life, do not truly desire the happy life. Or do all desire it, but because the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that they cannot do what they would, they fall back on what they can, and are content with that — because what they are not able to do, they do not will strongly enough to be made able? For I ask anyone whether he would rather rejoice in truth or in falsehood. They are as quick to say "in truth" as to say that they wish to be happy. For a happy life is joy in the truth: and this is joy in you, who are the Truth, O God my light, the health of my face, my God. This is the happy life that all desire; this life, which alone is happy, all desire; to rejoice in the truth, all desire. I have met many who would deceive; one who would be deceived, no one. Where, then, did they come to know this happy life, except where they came to know the truth? For they love the truth too, since they would not be deceived; and when they love a happy life, which is nothing but rejoicing in the truth, then they also love the truth — which they would not love unless there were some knowledge of it in their memory. Why, then, do they not rejoice in it? Why are they not happy? Because they are more strongly taken up with other things that have more power to make them miserable than that which they so faintly remember has power to make them happy. For there is still a little light in human beings; let them walk, let them walk, that the darkness not overtake them.

But why does "truth breed hatred," and why does the man of yours who preaches the truth become an enemy to them, although a happy life is loved, which is nothing but joy in the truth? It must be that truth is loved in such a way that those who love something else want what they love to be the truth; and because they would not be deceived, they refuse to be shown that they are. And so they hate the truth for the sake of the thing they have loved instead of the truth. They love truth when she gives light, and hate her when she reproves. For since they do not wish to be deceived and do wish to deceive, they love her when she shows herself to them, and hate her when she shows them to themselves. And so she repays them: those who do not wish to be exposed by her, she exposes against their will, while she herself is not exposed to them. Thus, even thus, does the mind of man — blind and sick, foul and ill-favored — wish to be hidden, while it wishes that nothing be hidden from it. But the opposite is given it: it is not hidden from the Truth, but the Truth is hidden from it. Yet even so, in its misery, it would rather rejoice in truths than in falsehoods. Happy, then, it will be, when, with no distraction in the way, it shall rejoice in that one Truth, by whom all things are true.

See what a vast field I have ranged over in my memory, seeking you, O Lord; and I have not found you outside it. Nor have I found anything about you that I have not kept in memory, ever since I learned you. For since I learned you, I have not forgotten you. For where I found Truth, there I found my God, who is the Truth itself, which since I learned it I have not forgotten. Since I learned you, then, you stay in my memory; and there I find you, when I call you to mind and delight in you. These are my holy delights, which you have given me in your mercy, looking on my poverty.

But where in my memory do you stay, O Lord — where there do you stay? What lodging have you made for yourself? What sanctuary have you built? You have given my memory this honor, to stay in it; but in what quarter of it you stay, that is what I am considering. For in thinking of you I passed beyond those parts of memory that the beasts have too, since I did not find you there among the images of bodily things; and I came to those parts where I had stored the feelings of my mind, and did not find you there either; and I entered into the very seat of my mind, which it has in my memory, since the mind remembers itself too, and you were not there. For as you are not a bodily image, nor the feeling of a living being — as when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, forget, and the like — so neither are you the mind itself, because you are the Lord God of the mind; and all these things change, but you remain unchangeable over all, and yet you have stooped to dwell in my memory, ever since I learned you. And why do I now look for the place in it where you dwell, as if there were places there? Sure I am that in it you dwell, since I have remembered you ever since I learned you, and there I find you when I call you to mind.

Where, then, did I find you, that I might learn you? For you were not in my memory before I learned you. Where, then, did I find you, that I might learn you, but in yourself, above me? Place there is none; we go backward and forward, and there is no place. Everywhere, O Truth, you give audience to all who ask counsel of you, and at once you answer all, though they ask your counsel on many different matters. Clearly you answer, though not all hear clearly. All consult you on whatever they will, though they do not always hear what they will. He is your best servant who looks not so much to hear from you the thing he himself wants, as rather to want the thing he hears from you.

Late have I loved you, O Beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you! And see, you were within, and I was outside, and out there I searched for you, and into those beautiful things you made I went plunging, deformed as I was. You were with me, but I was not with you. Things kept me far from you — things that would have no being at all unless they had it in you. You called and cried aloud and broke through my deafness. You flashed, you shone, and you scattered my blindness. You breathed fragrance, and I drew in my breath and now I pant for you. I tasted, and now I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I burned for your peace.

When I shall cling to you with my whole self, I will nowhere have sorrow or toil, and my life will be wholly alive, wholly filled with you. But now, since you lift up the one you fill, and I am not yet full of you, I am a burden to myself. Joys I should weep over fight against sorrows in which I should rejoice, and on which side the victory lies, I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have pity on me. My evil sorrows fight against my good joys, and on which side the victory lies, I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have pity on me. Woe is me! See, I do not hide my wounds; you are the Physician, I the sick; you are merciful, I am miserable. Is not the life of man on earth one long trial? Who wants troubles and hardships? You command them to be endured, not loved. No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it. For though he is glad that he endures, he would rather there were nothing for him to endure. In adversity I long for prosperity; in prosperity I dread adversity. What middle ground is there between the two, where the life of man is not all trial? Woe to the prosperities of this world, once and again, through dread of adversity and the spoiling of joy! Woe to the adversities of this world, once and again, and a third time, through longing for prosperity, and because adversity itself is hard, and may shatter our endurance! Is not the life of man on earth all trial, without any letup?

And all my hope is nowhere but in your exceedingly great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will. You command us to be continent. And when a man knew, as Scripture says, that no one can be continent unless God gives it, this too was part of wisdom — to know whose gift it is. For by continence we are gathered up and brought back into the One, from whom we had spilled out into the many. For he loves you too little who loves anything along with you, which he does not love for your sake. O Love, who are forever burning and never burned out, O Charity, my God, set me on fire! You command continence: give what you command, and command what you will.

Truly you command me to be continent from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. You commanded me to keep from unlawful intercourse; and as for marriage itself, you counseled something better than what you permitted. And since you gave it, it was done, even before I became a steward of your sacrament. But there still live in my memory — of which I have spoken so much — the images of such things, which my old habit fixed there; and they haunt me, powerless while I am awake, but in sleep so vivid that they bring not only pleasure but even consent, and something very like the act itself. So far does the illusion of the image prevail, in my soul and in my flesh, that while I am asleep these false visions persuade me to what, while I am awake, the real ones cannot. Am I not then myself, O Lord my God? And yet there is so great a difference between myself and myself, in that single moment in which I pass from waking to sleeping, or come back from sleeping to waking! Where, then, is reason, by which, awake, a man resists such suggestions, and stays unshaken even if the things themselves are pressed on him? Is it shut up with the eyes? Is it lulled asleep with the bodily senses? And how is it that often even in sleep we resist, and, mindful of our resolve and standing most chastely by it, give no assent to such enticements? And yet there is so great a difference that, when it happens otherwise, on waking we return to peace of conscience, and by that very difference we discover that it was not we who did what was somehow done in us — though we are sorry it was.

Are you not mighty, God Almighty, mighty enough to heal all the diseases of my soul, and by your more abundant grace to quench even the unclean stirrings of my sleep? You will increase your gifts in me more and more, O Lord, that my soul may follow me to you, disentangled from the birdlime of lust, so that it does not rebel against itself, and may not, even in dreams, so much as consent — let alone, through images of the senses, commit those shameful defilements even to the pollution of the flesh. For it is not hard for the Almighty, who is able to do above all that we ask or think, to bring it about that no such thing should have, over the pure affections even of a sleeper, the slightest influence — not even such as a mere thought would restrain — and to do this not only in this life but at my present age. But what I still am in this kind of my evil, I have confessed to my good Lord, rejoicing with trembling at what you have given me, and grieving at what is still unfinished in me, hoping that you will perfect your mercies in me to the point of perfect peace, which my outer and inner self shall have with you, when death is swallowed up in victory.

There is another evil of the day, which I wish were enough for it. For by eating and drinking we repair the daily wearing-down of the body, until you destroy both belly and food, when you shall slay my emptiness with a wonderful fullness and clothe this corruptible body with everlasting incorruption. But for now the necessity is sweet to me, and against that sweetness I fight, lest I be taken captive; and I wage a daily war by fasting, often bringing my body into subjection, and my pains are driven off by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are in a way pains; they burn and kill like a fever, unless the medicine of food comes to our aid. And since this medicine is at hand through the comforts of your gifts, with which land and water and air serve our weakness, our calamity gets called gratification.

You have taught me this — that I should bring myself to take food as I take medicine. But while I am passing from the discomfort of emptiness to the contentment of being filled, in that very passage the snare of lust lies in wait for me. For the passing itself is a pleasure, and there is no other way to pass to where we must needs pass. And though health is the reason for eating and drinking, a dangerous pleasure attaches itself as a companion, and most often tries to go in front, so that for its sake I may do what I say, or wish, I do for the sake of health. Nor do the two have the same measure: what is enough for health is too little for pleasure. And often it is uncertain whether it is the necessary care of the body still asking for sustenance, or a deceiving voluptuousness of greed offering its services. In this uncertainty the unhappy soul is glad, and there prepares an excuse to shield itself, glad that it is not clear what suffices for the moderation of health, so that under the cloak of health it may hide the business of gratification. These temptations I daily try to resist, and I call on your right hand, and bring my perplexities to you, because in this matter I have as yet no settled counsel.

I hear the voice of my God commanding: Do not let your hearts be weighed down with overindulgence and drunkenness. Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, that it does not come near me. But overeating sometimes creeps up on your servant; you will have mercy, that it may be put far from me. For no one can be continent unless you give it. Many things you give us when we pray for them; and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from you; indeed, we received it beforehand for this very purpose, that we might afterward know this. A drunkard I never was; but drunkards I have known made sober by you. From you it was, then, that those who never were such should not become such, as from you it was that those who had been such should not be so forever, and from you it was that both should know from whom it came. I heard another voice of yours: Do not go after your lusts, and turn away from your own pleasure. And by your favor I have heard a saying I have much loved: Neither if we eat shall we have the more, nor if we eat not shall we have the less — which is to say, neither will the one make me rich, nor the other wretched. I heard another too: I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content; I know how to abound, and how to suffer want; I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. Behold a soldier of the heavenly camp, not the dust that we are! But remember, Lord, that we are dust, and that of dust you made man; and he was lost, and is found. Nor could that man do this of himself, for he too, who said this by the breathing in of your inspiration, was of the same dust. "I can do all things," he says, "through him who strengthens me." Strengthen me, that I can. Give what you command, and command what you will. He confesses that he received, and when he glories, he glories in the Lord. Another I have heard begging that he might receive: Take from me, he says, the cravings of the belly — by which it appears, O my holy God, that you give, when what you command to be done is done.

You have taught me, good Father, that to the pure all things are pure, but that it is evil for the man who eats with offense; that every creature of yours is good, and nothing to be refused that is received with thanksgiving; that food does not commend us to God; that no one should judge us in food or drink; that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not, and the one who does not eat should not judge the one who does. These things I have learned — thanks be to you, praise be to you, my God, my Master, knocking at my ears, lighting up my heart. Deliver me out of all temptation. I do not fear uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of craving. I know that Noah was allowed to eat every kind of flesh that was good for food; that Elijah was fed with flesh; that John, gifted with a wonderful abstinence, was not defiled by feeding on the living creatures, the locusts, that were his food. And I know that Esau was tricked by his craving for lentils; that David blamed himself for craving a drink of water; and that our King was tempted not over flesh but over bread. And so the people in the wilderness too deserved to be rebuked, not for craving flesh, but because in their craving for food they murmured against the Lord.

Set, then, amid these temptations, I struggle daily against the appetite of eating and drinking. For this is not the kind of thing I can settle to cut off once for all and never touch again, as I could with unlawful intercourse. So the bridle of the throat must be held tempered between slackness and stiffness. And who is the man, O Lord, who is not at all carried beyond the bounds of need? Whoever he is, he is a great one; let him make your name great. But I am not such a one, for I am a sinful man. Yet I too magnify your name; and he who has overcome the world makes intercession to you for my sins, numbering me among the weak members of his body, because your eyes have seen what is still unfinished in me, and in your book all shall be written.

With the allurements of smells I am not much troubled. When they are absent, I do not miss them; when they are present, I do not refuse them; yet I am ever ready to do without them. So it seems to me; perhaps I am deceived. For there is a mournful darkness in which my own powers are hidden from me, so that my mind, questioning itself about its own strength, does not readily dare to trust itself; because even what is in it is mostly hidden, unless experience brings it out. And no one ought to feel secure in this life, the whole of which is called a trial — that the man who has been able to pass from worse to better may not likewise pass from better to worse. Our one hope, our one confidence, our one sure promise, is your mercy.

The delights of the ear had more firmly entangled and enslaved me, but you loosened me and set me free. Now, in those melodies which your words breathe life into, when they are sung with a sweet and skilled voice, I do find a little rest — yet not so as to be held there, but so that I can disengage myself when I will. Still, together with the words, which are their life and by which they gain admission into me, they seek in my affections a place of some honor, and I can hardly find one fitting for them. For at times I seem to myself to give them more honor than is right, when I feel that our minds are kindled to a flame of devotion more holily and more fervently by the holy words when they are sung like this than when they are not, and that all the affections of our spirit, each by a sweetness of its own, have their own proper measures in the voice and in song, stirred up by some hidden correspondence. But this contentment of the flesh, to which the soul must not be handed over to be weakened, often deceives me, when the sense does not so wait upon reason as patiently to follow her, but, though it was admitted only for her sake, strains even to run ahead of her and lead her. So in these things I sin without noticing, and only afterward become aware of it.

At other times, over-anxiously avoiding this very deception, I go wrong by too great strictness — sometimes so far as to wish the whole melody of the sweet music that is used for David's Psalter banished from my ears, and from the Church's too; and that way seems safer to me which I remember being often told of Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, who made the reader of the psalm utter it with so slight an inflection of the voice that it was nearer to speaking than to singing. And yet, when I remember the tears I shed at the singing of your Church in the early days of my recovered faith, and how even now I am moved not by the singing but by the things sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and the most fitting modulation, I acknowledge again the great usefulness of this practice. So I waver between the peril of pleasure and the proven wholesomeness, inclined rather — though without pronouncing any final verdict — to approve the practice of singing in church, so that through the delight of the ears weaker minds may rise to a feeling of devotion. Yet when it happens that I am more moved by the singing than by what is sung, I confess that I have sinned and deserve punishment, and then I would rather not hear the singer. See now my state! Weep with me, and weep for me, all you who keep your feelings within so ordered that good action follows. As for you who do not act, these things do not touch you. But you, O Lord my God, hear; look, and see, and have mercy, and heal me, you in whose presence I have become a question to myself; and that is my weakness.

There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, on which I must make my confession in the hearing of the ears of your temple, those brotherly and devout ears, and so finish with the temptations of the lust of the flesh, which still assail me as I groan deeply and long to be clothed with my dwelling that is from heaven. The eyes love beautiful and varied shapes, and bright and pleasing colors. Let these not occupy my soul; let God rather occupy it, who made these things — very good indeed, yet he is my good, not they. And these affect me, awake, the whole day long, nor is there any rest given me from them, as there is from sounds, sometimes in silence, when all voices cease. For this queen of colors, the light, bathing everything we see, wherever I am through the day, gliding past me in countless forms, soothes me even when I am busy with other things and not noticing it. And so strongly does it twine itself in that, if it is suddenly withdrawn, it is sought again with longing, and if it is absent long, it saddens the mind.

O Light, which Tobias saw when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life, and himself went before him with the feet of charity, never straying; or which Isaac saw, when his fleshly eyes, heavy and closed by old age, were granted the grace, unknowingly, to bless his sons, but by blessing to know them; or which Jacob saw, when he too, blind through great age, with an enlightened heart shed light, in the persons of his sons, on the future tribes of his people foreshadowed in them, and laid his hands, mystically crossed, on his grandsons by Joseph — not as their father by his outward eye corrected him, but as he himself inwardly discerned! This is the light; it is one, and all are one who see and love it. But that bodily light of which I spoke seasons the life of this world for its blind lovers with an enticing and dangerous sweetness. But those who know how to praise you for it — O God, Creator of all — take it up into your hymns, and are not taken up by it in their sleep. Such would I be. These seductions of the eyes I resist, lest the feet by which I walk on your way be ensnared; and I lift up my invisible eyes to you, that you would pluck my feet out of the snare. You pluck them out, again and again, for they are ensnared. You do not cease to pluck them out, while I often entangle myself in the snares laid on every side, because you who keep Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.

What countless trifles, made by all kinds of arts and crafts — in our clothes, shoes, vessels, and works of every sort, in pictures too and all kinds of images, far exceeding any necessary and moderate use or any pious meaning — have people added to tempt their own eyes, outwardly chasing what they themselves make, inwardly forsaking him by whom they themselves were made, and destroying what they themselves were made to be! But I, my God and my Glory, even from this raise a hymn to you, and consecrate praise to him who consecrates me, because those beautiful patterns which through people's souls pass into their skilled hands come from that Beauty which is above our souls, the Beauty for which my soul sighs day and night. But the makers and lovers of these outward beauties draw from there the rule for judging them, but not for using them. And he is there, though they do not perceive him — so that they might not wander off, but keep their strength for you, and not scatter it abroad on pleasures that wear the soul out. But I, though I say this and see it, entangle my steps in these outward beauties; yet you pluck me out, O Lord, you pluck me out, because your loving-kindness is before my eyes. For I am caught, to my misery, and you mercifully pluck me out — sometimes without my feeling it, when I had only lightly brushed against them, sometimes with pain, because I had stuck fast.

To this is added another kind of temptation, dangerous in still more ways. For besides that lust of the flesh which lies in the delight of all the senses and pleasures — and its slaves, going far from you, waste away and perish — the soul has, through the same bodily senses, a certain empty and prying desire, cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning, which delights not in the flesh but in making experiments through the flesh. Since this has its seat in the appetite for knowledge, and the eyes are the sense chiefly used for gaining knowledge, it is called, in the language of Scripture, the lust of the eyes. For seeing belongs properly to the eyes; yet we use this word of the other senses too, when we put them to the search for knowledge. We do not say, "Listen how it flashes," or "Smell how it glows," or "Taste how it shines," or "Feel how it gleams"; for all these are said to be seen. And yet we say not only "See how it shines," which the eyes alone can perceive, but also "See how it sounds," "See how it smells," "See how it tastes," "See how hard it is." And so the general experience of the senses, as I said, is called the lust of the eyes, because the office of seeing, in which the eyes hold first place, the other senses claim for themselves by way of likeness, whenever they go searching after any knowledge.

From this we can tell more clearly where pleasure and where curiosity is at work upon the senses; for pleasure seeks objects that are beautiful, melodious, fragrant, savory, soft, but curiosity seeks even the opposite of these, for the sake of trying them out — not to suffer annoyance, but out of the lust of making trial and knowing. For what pleasure is there in seeing, in a mangled corpse, something that makes you shudder? And yet, if one is lying nearby, people flock to it, to be made sad, to turn pale. They are afraid to see it even in their sleep — as though, when awake, anyone had forced them to see it, or any report of its beauty had drawn them there! So too with the other senses, which it would take long to go through. From this disease of curiosity come all those strange sights put on in the theater. From it people go on to search out the hidden powers of nature, which is beyond our purpose, knowledge that profits nothing, and which they desire for nothing but the knowing. From it too, with that same end of perverted knowledge, magical arts are pursued. From it, even in religion itself, God is tempted, when signs and wonders are demanded of him not desired for any good end, but merely to make trial.

In this so vast wilderness, full of snares and dangers, see how many of these I have cut off and thrust out of my heart, as you have given me to do, O God of my salvation. And yet when do I dare to say — since so many such things buzz on every side about our daily life — when do I dare to say that nothing of this sort holds my gaze or stirs an idle interest in me? True, the theaters no longer carry me away, nor do I care to know the courses of the stars, nor did my soul ever consult the spirits of the dead; all sacrilegious mysteries I detest. From you, O Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and single-hearted service, by what tricks and suggestions does the enemy work on me to make me desire some sign! But I beg you, by our King and by our pure and holy homeland, Jerusalem, that as all consenting to this is far from me, so may it ever be further and further still. And when I pray to you for the rescue of anyone, my aim and intention are far different. You give, and will give, that I should follow you willingly, doing what you will.

And yet, in how many of the pettiest and most contemptible things our curiosity is daily tempted, and how often we give way, who can count? How often we begin as if we were merely tolerating people telling pointless stories, so as not to offend the weak, and then by degrees we take an interest in them! I no longer go to the circus to watch a dog chasing a hare; but if, passing through a field, that chase happens to be going on, it may pull me away even from some weighty thought and draw me after it — not that I turn the body of my horse aside, yet I incline my mind that way. And unless you, having made me see my weakness, quickly warned me either to rise toward you out of that sight by some reflection, or to despise it altogether and pass on, I stand there dully fixed. What of this — when, sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider wrapping them up as they rush into her nets, often catches my attention? Is the thing different because these are small creatures? I go on from them to praise you, the wonderful Creator and Orderer of all things; but it was not this that first drew my attention. It is one thing to rise quickly, another not to fall. And of such things my life is full; and my one hope is your great and wonderful mercy. For when our heart becomes a storehouse of such things, and is loaded with crowds of this abundant emptiness, then our prayers too are often broken off and distracted by them, and while in your presence we direct the voice of our heart to your ears, this so great matter is cut short by the rushing in of who knows what idle thoughts.

And you know how far you have already changed me, you who first healed me of the lust to vindicate myself, that you might then forgive all the rest of my sins, and heal all my diseases, and redeem my life from corruption, and crown me with mercy and pity, and satisfy my desire with good things; you who curbed my pride with your fear and tamed my neck to your yoke. And now I bear it, and it is light to me, because so you promised, and so you have made it; and truly so it was, and I did not know it, when I was afraid to take it up.

But, O Lord, you who alone are Lord without pride, because you are the one true Lord, who has no lord over you — has this third kind of temptation also ceased in me, or can it cease through this whole life? I mean the wish to be feared and loved by others for no other end than that we may have in it a joy that is no joy. A miserable life, and an ugly boastfulness! From this above all it comes that people neither purely love nor purely fear you. And therefore you resist the proud and give grace to the humble; yes, you thunder down upon the ambitions of the world, and the foundations of the mountains tremble. For because certain offices of human society make it necessary to be loved and feared by others, the enemy of our true blessedness presses hard upon us, spreading everywhere his snares of "Well done, well done," so that, greedily snatching at them, we may be taken off guard, and sever our joy from your truth and set it in the deceptions of men, and find pleasure in being loved and feared not for your sake but in your place; and so, made like him, he may have us for his own, not in the bonds of love but in the bonds of punishment — he who set out to place his throne in the north, that dark and chilled we might serve him, perversely and crookedly imitating you. But we, O Lord, see, we are your little flock; possess us as yours, stretch your wings over us, and let us fly beneath them. Be our glory; let us be loved for your sake, and let your word be feared in us. Whoever would be praised by men when you blame him will not be defended by men when you judge him, nor delivered when you condemn him. But when a man is praised — not the sinner praised in the cravings of his soul, nor the man blessed who does wickedly, but a man praised for some gift you have given him — and he rejoices more in the praise of himself than that he has the gift for which he is praised, he too is praised while you find fault with him; and better is the one who praised than the one who is praised. For the one took pleasure in God's gift in a man; the other was better pleased with a man's gift than with God's.

By these temptations we are assailed daily, O Lord; without ceasing we are assailed. Our daily furnace is the tongue of men. And in this matter too you command us to be continent: give what you command, and command what you will. You know on this the groans of my heart and the floods of my eyes. For I cannot learn how far I have been cleansed of this plague, and I greatly fear my hidden sins, which your eyes know and mine do not. For in other kinds of temptation I have some means of examining myself; in this, scarcely any. For in restraining my mind from the pleasures of the flesh and from idle curiosity, I see how much I have gained when I do without them, foregoing them, or simply not having them; for then I ask myself how much more or less it troubles me not to have them. Riches, too, which are desired so that they may serve one or two or all of the three lusts — if the soul cannot tell whether, while it has them, it despises them, they can be cast aside, so that it may put itself to the test. But to be without praise, and so test our strength there, must we live badly — so abandonedly and atrociously that no one could know us without detesting us? What greater madness could be said or thought? But if praise is and ought to be the companion of a good life and good works, we ought as little to give up its company as the good life itself. And yet I do not know whether I can be well or ill without anything, unless it is taken from me.

What, then, do I confess to you in this kind of temptation, O Lord? What, but that I am delighted by praise — yet by truth itself more than by praise? For if it were put to me whether I would rather, raving in error about everything, be praised by everyone, or, steady and most settled in the truth, be blamed by everyone, I see which I would choose. Yet I wish that the approval of another did not even increase my joy at any good in me. But I admit it does increase it; and not only that, but blame diminishes it. And when I am troubled at this misery of mine, an excuse comes to me, of what worth, you, O God, know, for it leaves me uncertain. For since you have commanded us not only continence — that is, what to hold our love back from — but also righteousness, that is, where to bestow it, and have willed us to love not only you but our neighbor too, it often seems to me, when I am pleased by intelligent praise, that I am pleased at my neighbor's good sense or promise, or grieved at evil in him, when I hear him disparage either what he does not understand or what is good. For sometimes I am grieved at my own praise, either when things are praised in me which I dislike in myself, or when lesser and slight goods are valued more than they deserve. But again, how do I know whether I am thus affected because I do not want the one who praises me to differ from me about myself — not out of any concern for him, but because those same good things that please me in myself please me more when they please another as well? For in a way I am not praised, when my own judgment of myself is not praised; since either things are praised which displease me, or those more which please me less. Am I, then, in doubt about myself in this matter?

Behold, in you, O Truth, I see that I ought not to be moved by my own praises for my own sake, but for the good of my neighbor. And whether it is so with me, I do not know. For here I know less of myself than of you. I beg you now, O my God, show me to myself as well, that I may confess to my brothers, who are to pray for me, where I find myself crippled. Let me examine myself again, more carefully. If in my praise I am moved by my neighbor's good, why am I less moved if another is unjustly disparaged than if it is myself? Why am I more stung by an insult thrown at me than by one thrown, with equal injustice, at another in front of me? Do I not know this either? Or is it that at the last I deceive myself, and do not do the truth before you in heart and tongue? Put this madness far from me, O Lord, lest my own mouth be to me the sinner's oil to anoint my head. I am poor and needy, yet I am better while in hidden groanings I displease myself and seek your mercy, until what is lacking in my broken state is renewed and perfected, on to that peace which the eye of the proud does not know.

Yet the word that comes out of the mouth, and the deeds known to others, carry with them a most dangerous temptation through the love of praise, which, to establish a certain excellence of one's own, begs and gathers up the votes of men. It tempts even when it is reproved by me in myself, and on the very ground that it is reproved; and a man often glories more emptily over his very contempt of empty glory — so that it is no longer contempt of empty glory that he glories in, for he does not despise it when he glories.

Within, too, within is another evil, arising from a like temptation, by which people grow vain, pleasing themselves in themselves, though they please no one else, or displease or do not care to please others. But pleasing themselves, they greatly displease you, taking pleasure not only in things that are not good as though they were good, but in your good things as though they were their own; or, even if as yours, then as though earned by their own merits; or, even if as from your grace, yet not with brotherly rejoicing, but begrudging that grace to others. In all these and the like perils and labors you see the trembling of my heart, and I feel my wounds healed by you rather than not inflicted by me.

Where have you not walked with me, O Truth, teaching me what to beware of and what to desire, when I referred to you what I could discover here below, and consulted you? With my outward senses, as best I could, I surveyed the world, and observed the life that my body has from me, and these my senses. From there I entered the recesses of my memory, those manifold and spacious chambers, wonderfully filled with countless stores; and I considered, and stood aghast, able to discern none of these things without you, and finding none of them to be you. Nor was I myself, who found these things out, who went over them all and labored to sort them and to value each according to its worth — taking some on the report of my senses, questioning others that I felt to be mingled with myself, numbering and distinguishing the reporters themselves, and in the great treasure-house of my memory turning over some things, storing up others, drawing out others. Nor was I myself when I did this — that is, that power of mine by which I did it — nor was it you; for you are the abiding light, which I consulted about all these things, whether they were, what they were, and how to be valued; and I heard you directing and commanding me. And this I often do; this delights me, and as far as I can be freed from necessary duties, to this pleasure I have recourse. Nor in all these things which I run over, consulting you, can I find a safe place for my soul except in you, into whom my scattered members may be gathered, and nothing of me depart from you. And sometimes you admit me to a feeling deep within, most unusual, rising to a strange sweetness, which, if it were perfected in me, would be I know not what that does not belong to the life to come. But through my wretched burdens I sink down again into these lower things, and am swept back by old habit, and held fast; and I weep much, but am much held. So heavily does the weight of bad habit press us down. Here I can stay, but would not; there I would be, but cannot; miserable both ways.

So, then, I have considered the sicknesses of my sins in that threefold lust, and have called your right hand to my help. For with a wounded heart I have beheld your brightness, and, struck back, I said, "Who can reach there? I am cast away from before your eyes." You are the Truth, presiding over all; but I, in my greed, did not want to lose you, and yet wanted to possess a lie along with you — as no man wants to speak falsely in such a way as to be himself ignorant of the truth. And so I lost you, because you will not be possessed together with a lie.

Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Was I to have recourse to angels? With what prayers, with what rites? Many, trying to return to you and unable of themselves, have, so I hear, attempted this, and fallen into a craving for strange visions, and been thought worthy only to be deluded. For, being high-minded, they sought you by the pride of learning, puffing out their chests rather than beating their breasts; and so, by the kinship of their hearts, they drew to themselves the powers of the air, their fellow conspirators in pride, by whom, through magical influences, they were deceived, seeking a mediator by whom they might be cleansed, and there was none. For it was the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light. And it greatly enticed proud flesh that he had no body of flesh. For they were mortal and sinners, but you, Lord, to whom they proudly sought to be reconciled, are immortal and without sin. But a mediator between God and man must have something like God and something like men; for if in both respects he were like man, he would be far from God, and if in both like God, too unlike man — and so not a mediator. That deceitful mediator, then, by whom in your secret judgments pride deserved to be deluded, has one thing in common with man, namely sin; and another thing he would seem to have in common with God, for, not being clothed with the mortality of flesh, he would vaunt himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, this he has in common with men, that with them he should be condemned to death.

But the true Mediator, whom in your secret mercy you have shown to the humble, and have sent so that by his example too they might learn that same humility — that Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal with men, just with God; so that, because the wage of righteousness is life and peace, he might, by a righteousness joined to God, cancel the death of sinners now made righteous, the death he willed to share with them. Through him he was shown forth to the holy men of old, that they, by faith in his Passion to come, as we by faith in it now past, might be saved. For as man he was Mediator; but as the Word he is not in the middle between God and man, because he is equal to God, and God with God, and together one God.

How you have loved us, good Father, who did not spare your only Son, but gave him up for us ungodly ones! How you have loved us, for whom he, who thought it no robbery to be equal with you, was made subject even to the death of the cross — he, the only one free among the dead, having power to lay down his life and power to take it up again; for us to you both Victor and Victim, and therefore Victor because Victim; for us to you both Priest and Sacrifice, and therefore Priest because Sacrifice; making us, instead of servants, your sons, by being born of you and serving us. With reason, then, is my hope strong in him, that you will heal all my diseases through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us; otherwise I would despair. For many and great are my diseases, many and great; but your medicine is mightier. We might have thought your Word far removed from any union with man, and despaired of ourselves, had he not been made flesh and dwelt among us.

Terrified by my sins and the burden of my misery, I had turned it over in my heart and resolved to flee into the wilderness; but you forbade me, and strengthened me, saying: Therefore Christ died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them. See, Lord, I cast my care upon you, that I may live, and consider the wondrous things of your law. You know my unskillfulness and my weaknesses; teach me, and heal me. He, your only Son, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, has redeemed me with his blood. Let not the proud speak evil of me, because I meditate on my ransom, and eat and drink and share it abroad; and, poor, I desired to be filled from him among those who eat and are satisfied; and they shall praise the Lord who seek him.
books.title: Memory, and Late Have I Loved You

books.label: Book XI
paragraphs: Lord, since eternity is yours, can you be ignorant of what I tell you? Or do you see in time what happens in time? Then why do I lay before you, one after another, so many accounts of myself? Surely not so that you might learn them through me — but to stir up my own devotion toward you, and my readers', so that together we may say: Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. I have said it already, and I will say it again: I do this for love of your love. For we pray, too, and yet the Truth has said, Your Father knows what you need before you ask. So it is our hearts we lay open to you, confessing our miseries and your mercies upon us, that you may set us wholly free — since you have already begun — that we may stop being wretched in ourselves and be blessed in you, for you have called us to become poor in spirit, and meek, and mourners, hungering and thirsting after righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, peacemakers. See, I have told you many things, as well as I could and as much as I wished, because you first willed that I should confess to you, Lord my God. For you are good, and your mercy endures forever.

But how could I, with the pen for my tongue, ever utter all your urgings, all your warnings and comforts and guidings, by which you brought me to preach your Word and dispense your Sacrament to your people? And even if I could utter them in order, the drops of time are precious to me. For a long time I have burned to meditate on your law, and there to confess to you both my skill and my unskillfulness — the daybreak of your enlightening in me, and the leftover scraps of my darkness — until weakness is swallowed up in strength. I would not have anything else steal away the hours I find free of the needs of feeding my body and resting my mind, and of the service we owe to others, or that we pay even when we do not owe it.

Lord my God, give ear to my prayer, and let your mercy listen to my longing; for it is anxious not for myself alone, but would serve the love of my brothers — and you can see my heart, that this is so. Let me make a sacrifice to you of the work of my thought and my tongue; only give me what I may offer you. For I am poor and needy, and you are rich to all who call on you — you who are untouched by care, and yet care for us. Cut away from all rashness and all lying both my inner and my outer lips. Let your Scriptures be my pure delight; let me not be deceived in them, nor deceive out of them. Lord, listen and have pity, Lord my God, light of the blind, strength of the weak — and light of those who see, strength of the strong as well. Listen to my soul, and hear it crying out of the depths. For if your ears are not with us in the depths too, where shall we go? where cry out? The day is yours, the night is yours; at your nod the moments fly. Out of them grant us a space for meditating on the hidden things of your law, and do not shut it against us who knock. For it was not for nothing that you willed so many pages to be written with their shadowy secrets; those forests are not without their deer, which slip in among them and roam and walk, feed, lie down, and chew the cud. Make me whole, Lord, and unveil those secrets to me. Look — your voice is my joy; your voice outdoes a flood of pleasures. Give me what I love; for I do love, and this too you have given me. Do not forsake your own gifts, do not despise your green and thirsting blade of grass. Let me confess to you whatever I find in your books, and hear the voice of praise, and drink you in, and turn over the wonderful things in your law — from the very beginning, in which you made the heaven and the earth, all the way to the everlasting reign of your holy city with you.

Lord, have mercy on me, and hear my longing. For it is not, I think, of the earth — not of gold and silver, precious stones, fine clothes, honors and offices, pleasures of the flesh, or even the necessities for the body and for this pilgrim life of ours: all these things shall be added to those who seek your kingdom and your righteousness. See, Lord my God, where my longing lies. The wicked have told me of their delights, but none like your law, Lord. See where my longing lies. Look, Father — look, and see, and approve; let it be pleasing in the sight of your mercy that I find grace with you, that the inner depths of your words may be opened to me as I knock. I beg you by our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, the Man at your right hand, the Son of man whom you have made strong for yourself as the mediator between you and us, through whom you sought us when we were not seeking you — sought us, so that we might seek you; your Word, through whom you made all things, and me among them; your Only-Begotten, through whom you called your believing people to adoption, and me among them. I beg you by him who sits at your right hand and pleads with you for us, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. These are the treasures I seek in your books. Of him Moses wrote; this he says himself; this says the Truth.

I want to hear and understand how, in the Beginning, you made the heaven and the earth. Moses wrote this; he wrote and went on his way, passing from you to you; and he is not here before me now. For if he were, I would catch hold of him and ask him, and beg him by you to open these things to me, and lay the ears of my body to the sounds bursting from his mouth. But if he spoke Hebrew, it would strike my senses in vain — none of it would reach my mind; if Latin, I would know what he said. But how would I know whether he spoke the truth? And even if I knew that, would I know it from him? No — within me, deep within, in the chamber of my thoughts, Truth, which is neither Hebrew nor Greek nor Latin nor any foreign tongue, with no apparatus of voice or tongue, no sound of syllables, would say, It is true; and at once I would say, with all confidence, to that man of yours, You speak the truth. But since I cannot question him, it is you I beg — you, Truth, with whom he was full when he spoke truth — you, my God, I beg: forgive my sins; and you who gave your servant the gift of speaking these things, give me also the gift of understanding them.

Look: the heavens and the earth exist; they cry out that they were created, for they change and vary. But whatever has not been made, and yet exists, has nothing in it that it did not have before — and to have such a difference is exactly what it means to change and vary. They cry out, too, that they did not make themselves: We exist, because we have been made; we did not exist before we existed, so as to give ourselves being. And the proof is the plain voice of the things that say it. You, then, Lord, made them — you who are beautiful, for they are beautiful; you who are good, for they are good; you who are, for they are. And yet they are not beautiful, not good, not even fully real, as you their Creator are: set beside you, they are neither beautiful nor good nor real at all. This we know — and thanks be to you for it. And our knowledge, set beside your knowledge, is ignorance.

But how did you make the heaven and the earth? What was the engine of so vast a work? You did not work as a human craftsman does, shaping one body out of another at the discretion of his mind, which can somehow cast over the new thing a form it sees within itself by its inward eye. And how would he be able to do even that, unless you had made his mind? He casts a form over what already exists and already has being — clay, or stone, or wood, or gold, or the like. And how would those exist, had you not appointed them? You made the craftsman his body; you made the mind that commands the limbs; you made the matter out of which he makes anything; you made the grasp by which he takes in his art and sees within what he is to do without; you made the senses of his body, by which, as by an interpreter, he carries over from mind to matter what he is making, and reports back to his mind what is done, so that the mind may consult within the Truth that presides over it, whether the thing is well done or not. All these praise you, the Creator of all. But how do you make them? How, God, did you make heaven and earth? Surely not in the heaven, nor in the earth, did you make heaven and earth; nor in the air or the waters, since these too belong to heaven and earth; nor in the whole world did you make the whole world, since there was no place to make it in, before it was made, that it might be. Nor did you hold anything in your hand out of which to make heaven and earth. For where would you have gotten this thing you had not yet made, to make anything from? For what is there at all, except because you are? So you spoke, and they were made; and in your Word you made them.

But how did you speak? In the way the voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son? For that voice went by and went away — it began and ended; the syllables sounded and passed, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so on in order, until the last after all the rest, and silence after the last. From which it is perfectly plain that it was the motion of a creature that uttered it — a motion that is itself in time, in service to your eternal will. And these words of yours, made for a moment, the outward ear reported to the discerning soul, whose inward ear was listening to your eternal Word. But the soul compared these words sounding in time with that eternal Word of yours in its silence, and said: It is different — utterly different. These words are far beneath me; in fact they are not, for they flee and pass away; but the Word of my Lord abides above me forever. So if it was in sounding, passing words that you said heaven and earth should be made, and thus made heaven and earth, then there was some bodily creature before heaven and earth, by whose motions in time that voice could run its course in time. But there was no bodily thing before heaven and earth; or if there was, then surely you had created it — without any such passing voice — out of which to make the passing voice by which to say, Let the heaven and the earth be made. For whatever that was, out of which such a voice was made, unless you had made it, it could not have existed at all. By what Word, then, did you speak, so that a body might come to be, by which these words could in turn be made?

So you call us to understand the Word, the God who is God with you, who is spoken eternally, and by whom all things are spoken eternally. For what is spoken is not spoken one thing after another, each finished so that the next may be spoken, but all things together and eternally. Otherwise we already have time and change — and not a true eternity, not a true immortality. This I know, my God, and I give thanks. I know it, I confess it to you, Lord; and along with me, anyone who is not ungrateful to certain Truth knows it and blesses you. We know it, Lord, we know it: insofar as a thing is not what it was, and is what it was not, just so far it dies and rises. Nothing of your Word, then, gives place or takes the place of another, because it is truly immortal and eternal. And so to the Word coeternal with you, you say all at once and eternally everything you say; and whatever you say shall be made, is made; nor do you make in any way except by speaking. And yet the things you make by speaking are not made all at once, and are not everlasting.

Why is this, I beg you, Lord my God? I see it after a fashion, but how to put it into words I do not know — unless it is this: that whatever begins to be, and stops being, begins and stops just then, when in your eternal Reason it is known that it ought to begin or to stop — in which Reason nothing begins or stops. This is your Word, which is also the Beginning, because it also speaks to us. So in the Gospel he speaks through the flesh, and this sounded outwardly in the ears of men, so that it might be believed and sought inwardly, and found in the eternal Truth, where the good and only Master teaches all his disciples.
