There, Lord, I hear your voice speaking to me; for the one who teaches us is the one who speaks to us, and the one who does not teach us, even when he speaks, does not speak to us. And who teaches us but the unchanging Truth? For even when we are warned through some changeable creature, we are only being led to the unchanging Truth, where we truly learn when we stand and listen to him and rejoice greatly because of the Bridegroom's voice, which gives us back to the One from whom we are. And therefore he is the Beginning: for unless he stayed fast, there would be, when we went astray, no place to return to. But when we return from our wandering, it is by knowing that we return; and so that we may know, he teaches us, because he is the Beginning, and speaks to us.

In this Beginning, God, you made heaven and earth — in your Word, in your Son, in your Power, in your Wisdom, in your Truth — speaking in a wondrous way and making in a wondrous way. Who can grasp it? Who can tell it? What is this that flickers through me and strikes my heart without wounding it, so that I shudder and burn? I shudder, because I am unlike it; I burn, because I am like it. It is Wisdom — Wisdom herself — that flickers through me, parting the cloud over me, the cloud that mantles me again as I faint away from her, into the darkness that gathers on me for my punishment. For my strength has been worn down to nothing, so that I cannot bear my own blessings, until you, Lord, who have been gracious to all my wrongs, heal all my weaknesses. For you will redeem my life from ruin, and crown me with loving-kindness and tender mercy, and satisfy my longing with good things, because my youth shall be renewed like an eagle's. For in hope we are saved, and so we wait in patience for your promises. Let anyone who is able hear you speaking within him out of your own oracle. I will cry out boldly: How wonderful are your works, Lord; in Wisdom you have made them all. And this Wisdom is the Beginning, and in that Beginning you made heaven and earth.

Now look — are they not full of their old leaven, those who say to us: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? For if (they say) he was idle and doing nothing, then why does he not stay idle from now on and forever, just as he did before? For if some new motion arose in God, and a new will to make a creature he had never made before, then how could that be a true eternity, in which a will arises that was not there before? For the will of God is no creature; it comes before any creature, since nothing could be created unless the Creator's will came first. So the will of God belongs to his very being. And if something arose in God's being that was not there before, then that being cannot truly be called eternal. But if it was God's will from eternity that the creature should exist, then why was the creature itself not from eternity?

Whoever talks like this does not yet understand you, Wisdom of God, Light of minds; they do not yet understand how the things are made that are made through you and in you, and yet they strain to comprehend things eternal — while their heart flutters back and forth among the motions of past and future, and is still unsettled. Who will hold it still and fix it in place, so that it may stand still for a moment and catch, for a moment, the splendor of that ever-fixed Eternity, and set it beside the times that are never fixed, and see that there is no comparison? Who will make it see that a long time becomes long only out of many passing motions that cannot be stretched out all at once; that in the Eternal nothing passes, but the whole is present, whereas no stretch of time is ever wholly present at once; that all time past is driven on by time to come, and all that is to come follows on what is past, and all of it, past and future, is created and flows out of that which is always present? Who will hold still the heart of man, so that it may stand and see how the standing-still Eternity, which is neither past nor future, gives the orders to times past and to come? Can my hand do this — can the hand of my mouth, by speaking, bring about a thing so great?

See, I answer the man who asks, What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? I do not answer the way someone is said to have done — dodging the force of the question with a joke — He was preparing hell for those who pry into deep things. It is one thing to answer a question, another to make sport of the questioner. So I will not answer that way. I would rather answer I do not know to what I do not know, than say something that earns a laugh at a man asking about deep things, and praise for a man giving false answers. No — I say that you, our God, are the Creator of every creature; and if by the name heaven and earth we mean every creature, then I say boldly: before God made heaven and earth, he was not making anything. For if he was making something, what would he have been making but a creature? And I wish I knew everything I want to know for my good as surely as I know this: that no creature was made before any creature was made.

But suppose some restless mind goes roving over the images of bygone times, and marvels that you, God Almighty, the All-creating and All-sustaining, the Maker of heaven and earth, held back from so great a work through countless ages before you would make it. Let such a mind wake up and see that it is marveling at things that are false. For how could countless ages pass by that you did not make, you the Author and Creator of all ages? What times could there be that were not made by you? And how could they pass by, if they never were? Since, then, you are the Creator of all times, if there was any time before you made heaven and earth, why do they say you were keeping back from work? That very time you made yourself, and no times could pass by before you made those times. But if before heaven and earth there was no time, why ask what you were doing then? For there was no then, when there was no time.

And you do not precede time by time — otherwise you would not precede all times. No, you precede all things past by the height of an ever-present eternity, and you outlast all things to come, because they are still to come, and once they have come they will be past; but you are the Same, and your years do not fail. Your years neither come nor go; ours both come and go, so that they may all come at last. Your years all stand together, because they stand still; the years coming on do not thrust out the years departing, because none of them pass away — but ours will all have been only when none of them are any longer. Your years are a single day; and your day is not a day-after-day, but Today, since your Today does not give way to a tomorrow, nor does it follow on a yesterday. Your Today is Eternity; and so you begot the Coeternal, to whom you said, Today I have begotten you. You made all things, and you are before all times; and there was no time in which there was no time.

There was no time, then, in which you had not made anything, since time itself you made. And no times are coeternal with you, because you stand fast; whereas if they stood fast, they would not be times. For what is time? Who can explain it easily and briefly? Who can even grasp it in thought clearly enough to put it into words? And yet what do we mention in conversation more familiarly, more knowingly, than time? We understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it, too, when we hear someone else speak of it. So what is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Yet I say boldly that I know this much: that if nothing passed away, there would be no past time; that if nothing were coming, there would be no future time; and that if nothing were, there would be no present time. Those two times, then — past and future — how can they be, when the past is now not, and the future is not yet? But the present, if it were always present and never slid away into the past, would not be time at all, but eternity. So if the present, in order to be time, comes into being only because it slips away into the past, how can we say that it is, when the very ground of its being is that it will not be — so that we cannot truly say that time is, except because it is tending not to be?

And yet we say a long time and a short time, though only of the past or the future. A long time past, for instance, we call a hundred years ago; a long time to come, a hundred years from now. A short time past, say, ten days ago; a short time to come, ten days from now. But in what sense is that long or short, which does not exist? For the past is no longer, and the future is not yet. So let us not say it is long; let us say of the past, it has been long, and of the future, it will be long. My Lord, my Light — will not your Truth make a mockery of man here too? For that past time which was long: was it long when it was already past, or when it was still present? For it could only be long when there was something there that could be long; but once it was past, it no longer was, and so it could not be long, since it was not at all. Let us not say, then, time past has been long; for we will find nothing that has been long, since once it is past, it is no more. Let us say instead: that present time was long — because, while it was present, it was long. For it had not yet passed away into nonexistence, and so there was something that could be long. But once it was past, it stopped being long, because it stopped being.

Let us see, then, soul of man, whether present time can be long — for it is to you that the feeling and the measuring of length of time is given. What will you answer me? Are a hundred years, when present, a long time? But first see whether a hundred years can be present at all. If the first of those years is now running, it is present, but the other ninety-nine are still to come, and so are not yet. If the second year is running, one is already past, one present, the rest to come. And whatever middle year of the hundred we suppose to be present, all the years before it are past, all after it to come; so a hundred years cannot be present. But see at least whether the one year now running is itself present. If its first month is running, the rest are to come; if the second, the first is already past and the rest are not yet. So the year now running is not present as a whole; and if not present as a whole, then the year is not present. For twelve months make a year, and whichever month is running is present, while the rest are past or to come. Though in fact that running month is not present either, but only one day of it: if it is the first day, the rest are to come; if the last, they are past; if any day in between, then it stands between past and future.

See how the present time — the only one we found that could be called long — is shrunk to the length of barely a single day. But let us look even at that, because not even one day is present as a whole. For it is made up of twenty-four hours of night and day: the first hour has the rest still to come, the last has them all past, and any middle hour has those before it past and those after it to come. And that single hour itself is fleeing away in flying particles: whatever of it has flown off is past, whatever remains is to come. If we could conceive some instant of time that cannot be divided into even the smallest particles of moments, that alone is what could be called present — and yet it flies so fast from future into past that it cannot be stretched out with the least pause. For if it is stretched out, it is divided into past and future. The present has no length. Where, then, is the time we may call long? Is it the future? Of the future we do not say it is long, because it is not yet, so as to be long; we say it will be long. But when will it be? For if even then, while it is still to come, it shall not be long (because what can be long is not yet), and so it shall be long only when, out of the future that is not yet, it begins now to be and has become present — so that then there is something that can be long — then present time cries out, in the very words above, that it cannot be long.

And yet, Lord, we do perceive intervals of time, and compare them, and say some are shorter, others longer. We even measure how much longer or shorter one time is than another, and we answer: this is double, or triple; that is just once over, or only just as long as the other. But it is times as they are passing that we measure, by perceiving them; for who can measure times past, which now are not, or times to come, which are not yet — unless someone dares to claim that what does not exist can be measured? So while time is passing, it can be perceived and measured; but once it is past, it cannot, because then it is not.

I am asking, Father, not asserting: my God, rule me and guide me. Who will tell me there are not three times, the way we learned as boys and taught the boys after us — past, present, and future — but only the present, since the other two are not? Or are they too? And when the future becomes present, does it come out of some hidden place; and when it retreats, does present become past by going into hiding? For where did those who foretold things to come see them, if as yet they were not? What does not exist cannot be seen. And those who tell of things past could not tell of them if they did not somehow make them out in the mind; and if those things were nothing, they could in no way be made out. Things past, then, and things to come — they are.

Allow me, Lord, to search further. My hope, do not let my purpose be confounded. For if times past and future exist, I want to know where they are. And if I cannot grasp that, still I know this much: wherever they are, they are not there as future or as past, but as present. For if they are there as future, they are not yet there; if there as past, they are no longer there. Wherever they are, then, whatever they are, they are only as present. It is true that when we tell of past facts, what is drawn out of the memory is not the things themselves, which are gone, but words conceived from the images of those things — images they printed on the mind, in passing, by way of the senses, like footprints. My childhood, for instance, which now is not, lies in time past, which now is not; but when I call up its image and speak of it, I look on that image in the present, because it is still in my memory. Whether there is some like cause for the foretelling of things to come — so that images of things which as yet are not could be perceived beforehand, as already existing — I confess, my God, I do not know. This much I do know: that we generally think ahead about our future actions, and that this forethinking is present, but the action we are forethinking is not yet, because it is still to come. And once we have set about it and have begun to do what we were forethinking, then that action will be, because then it is no longer future but present.

Whatever the way may be, then, of this hidden fore-perceiving of things to come, nothing can be seen except what is. But what now is, is not future but present. So when things to come are said to be seen, it is not the things themselves that are seen — for as yet they are not — but perhaps their causes or signs, which already are. So they are not future to those who see them, but present; and out of them the future, conceived beforehand in the mind, is foretold. These conceptions, again, exist now; and those who foretell the things behold the conceptions present before them. Out of the countless variety of things, let one example serve me. I look at the daybreak; I announce that the sun is about to rise. What I look at is present; what I announce is to come. Not the sun, which already is, but its rising, which is not yet. And yet, unless I pictured that sunrise itself in my mind — as I do now while I speak of it — I could not foretell it. But neither is that daybreak which I make out in the sky the sunrise, though it goes before it; nor is the picture in my mind the sunrise: those two are seen now, in the present, so that the sunrise still to come may be foretold. Things to come, then, are not yet; and if they are not yet, they are not; and if they are not, they cannot be seen. Yet they can be foretold out of present things, which already are and are seen.

You, then, Ruler of your creation — by what way do you teach souls the things to come? For you did teach your prophets. By what way do you teach things to come, you to whom nothing is to come — or rather, out of things future, teach things present? For what does not exist cannot be taught. This way is too far beyond my sight; it is too mighty for me, I cannot reach it. But from you I can, when you grant it — sweet light of my hidden eyes.

What is clear and plain now is this: that neither things to come nor things past are. Nor is it strictly right to say there are three times, past, present, and to come. It might more strictly be said that there are three times: a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future. For these three do exist, after a fashion, in the soul, and nowhere else do I see them: the present of things past is memory; the present of things present is direct sight; the present of things future is expectation. If we are allowed to speak this way, then I do see three times, and I admit there are three. Let it also be said, in our loose way, that there are three times, past, present, and to come. See, I do not object, I do not argue, I find no fault — provided that what is said is understood, that neither what is to be now is, nor what is past. For there are few things we say strictly; most things we say loosely, and still the meaning gets across.

I said just now that we measure times as they pass, so as to be able to say that this stretch of time is twice as long as that, or just as long as that, and so on for any measurable parts of time. So, as I said, we measure times as they pass. And if anyone should ask me, How do you know? I might answer, I know that we do measure them; and that we cannot measure what is not; and that things past and to come are not. But present time — how do we measure it, since it has no length? It is measured while passing; once it has passed, it is not measured, for then there will be nothing there to measure. But where does it come from, by what way does it go, and where does it go, while it is being measured? Where from, but the future? By what way, but the present? Where to, but the past? From that which is not yet, then, through that which has no length, into that which now is not. And yet what is it we measure, if not time in some kind of length? For we do not say single, double, triple, equal, or any other such thing of time, except of lengths of time. In what length, then, do we measure time as it passes? In the future, where it comes from? But what is not yet, we cannot measure. In the present, where it goes by? But a thing with no length we cannot measure. In the past, where it goes to? But what now is not, we cannot measure either.

My soul is on fire to know this tangled riddle. Do not lock it away, Lord my God, good Father — through Christ I beg you — do not lock these things, familiar and yet hidden, away from my longing, so that it is barred from breaking through to them; but let them dawn for me by your enlightening mercy, Lord. Whom shall I ask about these things? And to whom would it do me more good to confess my ignorance than to you, to whom these studies of mine, so fiercely kindled toward your Scriptures, are no trouble? Give me what I love; for I do love, and this love too you gave me. Give, Father — you who truly know how to give good gifts to your children — give, because I have set myself to know, and the labor is before me until you open the way. Through Christ I beg you, in his name, the Holy of holies: let no one interrupt me. For I have believed, and so I speak. This is my hope, this is what I live for: to contemplate the delights of the Lord. See, you have made my days a span of years, and they pass away, and how, I do not know. And we talk of time and time, of times and times — How long ago since he said this; how long since he did that; how long since I saw such a thing; and this syllable lasts twice as long as that single short one. These words we speak, and these we hear, and we are understood, and we understand. They are utterly plain and ordinary, and yet the same things are too deeply hidden, and the discovery of them would be something new.

I once heard from a learned man that the motions of the sun, moon, and stars are what time is — and I did not agree. For why should the motions of all bodies, rather, not be time? Suppose the lights of heaven were to stop, and a potter's wheel went on turning: would there be no time by which to measure its turnings, and say that it turned at even intervals, or, if it ran sometimes slower and sometimes faster, that some rounds took longer and others less? And while we were saying this, would we not ourselves be speaking in time? And would there not be in our words some syllables short, some long — short because they sounded in a shorter time, long because in a longer? God, grant to men to see, in a small thing, what holds true of things great and small alike. There are stars and lights of heaven for signs and seasons, for years and days; there they are. Yet I would not say that the turning of that wooden wheel was a day, nor would he be right to say it was therefore no time at all.

I want to know the force and nature of time, by which we measure the motions of bodies and say, for instance, this motion is twice as long as that. For here is my question. A day does not mean only the sun's stay above the earth — by which day is one thing and night another — but also its whole circuit from east round to east again, by which we say so many days have passed, the nights included when we say so many days, and not counted apart. Since, then, a day is completed by the sun's motion, by its circuit from east round to east, I ask: is it the motion alone that makes the day, or the stretch of time in which that motion is completed, or both? If the first, then we would have a day even if the sun finished that course in as small a space as one hour. If the second, then it would not make a day if there were only as short a stay as one hour between one sunrise and the next, but the sun would have to go round twenty-four times to complete a single day. If both, then it could not be called a day either if the sun ran its whole round in the space of one hour, nor if, while the sun stood still, as much time went by as the sun usually takes to make its whole course from one morning to the next. So I will not ask now what it is that we call a day, but what time itself is — that time by which, measuring the sun's circuit, we could say it was finished in half the usual time, if it ran its course in as small a space as twelve hours; and, comparing the two times, could call this one a single time and that a double — even supposing the sun ran its round from east to east sometimes in the single time, sometimes in the double. So let no one tell me that the motions of the heavenly bodies are time, since once, at one man's prayer, the sun stood still until he could win his battle: the sun stood still, but time went on. For in its own allotted span of time that battle was fought and finished. I see, then, that time is a kind of stretching-out. But do I really see it, or only seem to? You, my Light and my Truth, will show me.

Do you tell me to agree, if someone defines time as the motion of a body? You do not. For that no body is moved except in time, I hear — this you say; but that the motion of a body is time, I do not hear; this you do not say. For when a body is moved, it is by time that I measure how long it moves, from when it began until it stopped. And if I did not see where it began, and it kept moving so that I did not see when it stopped, I cannot measure it — except, perhaps, from the time I began watching until I stopped. And if I watch long, I can only say it is a long time, not how long; for when we say how long, we say it by comparison: this is as long as that, or twice as long as that, and the like. But when we can mark the distances of the places the moving body goes from and to — or the distances its parts go, if it turns like a wheel on a lathe — then we can say exactly in how much time the motion of that body, or of its part, from this place to that, was finished. Since, then, the motion of a body is one thing, and that by which we measure how long the motion is, another, who does not see which of the two ought rather to be called time? For if a body is sometimes moving and sometimes standing still, we measure by time not only its motion but its standing still as well, and say it stood still as long as it moved, or twice or three times as long as it moved, or whatever other length our measuring has fixed, or guessed at — more or less, as we say. Time, then, is not the motion of a body.

And I confess to you, Lord, that I still do not know what time is. And again I confess to you, Lord, that I know I am saying this in time, and that I have been speaking of time for a long while, and that this very long while is long only by the passing of time. So how do I know this, when I do not know what time is? Or is it perhaps that I do not know how to put into words what I do know? How wretched I am, that I do not even know what I do not know! See, my God, I do not lie before you: as I speak, so is my heart. You will light my lamp; you, Lord my God, will brighten my darkness.

Does not my soul confess to you, most truly, that I do measure times? And so, my God, I measure, and I do not know what I am measuring? I measure the motion of a body by time — and time itself, do I not measure that? But could I really measure how long a body moves, and in how long a stretch of time it goes from this place to that, without measuring the time in which it moves? So this time itself, how do I measure it? Do we measure a longer time by a shorter, as we measure the length of a beam by the length of a forearm? For that does seem to be how we measure the length of a long syllable by a short one, and say it is double. In just this way we measure the length of a stanza by the lengths of its lines, the lengths of the lines by the lengths of the feet, the lengths of the feet by the lengths of the syllables, the lengths of long syllables by the lengths of short — not measuring by pages (for that way we measure spaces, not times), but as the words are uttered and pass by, when we say: it is a long stanza, because made of so many lines; long lines, because made of so many feet; long feet, because drawn out by so many syllables; a long syllable, because double a short one. But not even this way do we get any sure measure of time, because it may happen that a shorter line, pronounced slowly, takes up more time than a longer one rushed through — and the same for a foot, a syllable. From all this it seemed to me that time is nothing other than a stretching-out — but of what, I do not know, and I would be amazed if it were not a stretching of the mind itself. For what is it, I beg you, my God, that I measure, when I say, vaguely, this time is longer than that, or, exactly, this is double that? That I measure time, I know; and yet I do not measure the future, for it is not yet; nor the present, because it has no length; nor the past, because it now is not. What, then, do I measure? Times as they pass, not times that have passed? For so I said.

Courage, my mind, and press on hard. God is our helper; he made us, and not we ourselves. Press on where the truth begins to dawn. Suppose the sound of a voice begins, and sounds, and goes on sounding, and then — listen — it stops; now there is silence, and the voice is past, and is no longer a voice. Before it sounded, it was to come, and could not be measured, because as yet it was not; and now it cannot be measured, because it no longer is. So while it was sounding it could be, because then there was something that could be measured. But even then it was not standing still, for it was passing on and passing away. Was it the more measurable for that? For as it passed, it was being stretched out into some length of time, so that it could be measured, since the present has no length. So if it could be measured then — see, suppose another voice has begun, and is still sounding on in one unbroken stretch without a break. Let us measure it while it sounds; for once it has stopped sounding it will be past, and there will be nothing left to measure. Let us measure it, then, and say how long it is. But it is still sounding, and it cannot be measured except from where it began to where it left off. For the very interval between is the thing we measure — from some beginning to some end. So a voice that is not yet ended cannot be measured, in such a way that one could say how long or short it is, or call it equal to another, or double a single one. But once it is ended, it no longer is. How, then, can it be measured? And yet we do measure times — not those which are not yet, nor those which no longer are, nor those that are not stretched out by any pause, nor those that have no bounds. We measure neither times to come, nor past, nor present, nor passing; and still we do measure times.

Deus Creator omnium — God, Creator of all: this verse of eight syllables alternates between short and long. The four short ones, the first, third, fifth, and seventh, are single, against the four long, the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth; each of these long ones takes double the time of each short one. I pronounce them, I report on them, and I find it so, as plain hearing perceives. By plain hearing, then, I measure a long syllable by a short, and I plainly find it to last twice as long. But when one sounds after the other — the short one first, the long one after — how am I to hold on to the short one, and how, in measuring, am I to lay it against the long one, so as to find that the long has twice as much, seeing that the long does not begin to sound until the short has stopped? And that long syllable itself — do I measure it while it is present, when I do not measure it until it is ended? And its ending is its passing away. So what is it I measure? Where is the short syllable I measure by? Where the long one I measure? Both have sounded, have flown off, have passed away, are gone; and yet I measure, and I answer with confidence — as far as a practiced ear can be trusted — that this syllable is single, that one double, in length of time. And I could not do this unless they were already past and ended. So it is not the syllables themselves, which now are not, that I measure, but something that stays fixed in my memory.

It is in you, my mind, that I measure times. Do not interrupt me — that is, do not interrupt yourself with the uproar of your own impressions. In you I measure times. The impression that things make on you as they pass remains when they are gone; it is this present impression that I measure, not the things that passed by to make it. This is what I measure when I measure times. So either this is time, or I am not measuring time at all. And what of when we measure silence, and say this silence lasted as long as that voice did? Do we not stretch out our thought to the measure of the voice, as if it were sounding, so as to be able to report on the intervals of silence in a given length of time? For though voice and tongue are still, in thought we go over poems and verses and any other discourse, and over the spans of any motions, and we report on their lengths of time, how much this is in relation to that, exactly as if we were uttering them aloud. If a man wants to make a long sound, and has settled in thought how long it is to be, that man has already gone through a length of time in silence, and, committing it to memory, he begins to utter the sound, which goes on sounding until it is brought to the end he set for it. Indeed it has sounded, and it will sound; for as much of it as is finished has already sounded, and the rest will sound. And so it goes on, until present attention carries the future over into the past, the past growing as the future shrinks, until, when the future is wholly used up, the whole is past.

But how is that future shrunk or used up, when it is not yet? And how is the past made to grow, when it is no longer? Only because, in the mind that does all this, there are three things going on. For it expects, and it attends, and it remembers, so that what it expects passes, by way of what it attends to, into what it remembers. Who would deny that things to come are not yet? And yet there is in the mind an expectation of things to come. Who would deny that things past are now no longer? And yet there is still in the mind a memory of things past. And who would deny that the present time has no length, since it passes away in an instant? And yet attention lasts on, and through it what shall be present goes on its way to become no longer present. So it is not future time that is long, for it is not yet; a long future is a long expectation of the future. Nor is it past time that is long, for it now is not; a long past is a long memory of the past.

I am about to recite a psalm I know. Before I begin, my expectation reaches out over the whole; but once I have begun, whatever I pluck off from it into the past reaches out along my memory; and so the life of this act of mine is stretched two ways — into memory, as to what I have already said, and into expectation, as to what I am about to say. But attention is present all the while, and through it what was future is carried over to become past. And the more this goes on and on, the more expectation is shortened and memory is lengthened, until the whole expectation is used up, when the whole act is finished and has passed over into memory. And what happens in the whole psalm happens also in each of its parts and each of its syllables; it happens in the longer action of which this psalm may be a part; it happens in the whole life of a man, of which all his actions are parts; it happens across the whole age of the sons of men, of which all the lives of men are parts.

But because your loving-kindness is better than all our lives, see, my life is nothing but a being-pulled-apart; and your right hand has held me up, in my Lord the Son of man, the Mediator between you, the One, and us the many — many, and scattered too among many things. Through him may I lay hold of the One in whom I have been laid hold of, and be gathered up out of my old days, to follow the One — forgetting what lies behind, and not stretched out and torn between what shall be and what shall pass away, but reaching toward the things that are before me, and not by being pulled apart but by straining forward, I press on for the prize of my heavenly calling, where I may hear the voice of your praise and contemplate your delight, which neither comes nor passes away. But now my years are spent in mourning, and you, Lord, are my comfort, my Father everlasting; while I have been broken apart among times whose order I do not know, and my thoughts, the very inmost depths of my soul, are torn and mangled with their tumult of changes, until I flow together into you, refined and melted down in the fire of your love.

And then I will stand still, and grow firm in you — in my mould, your truth; and I will not put up with the questions of men who, by a sickness they have earned, thirst for more than they can hold, and say: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? Or, How did it come into his mind to make something, when he had never made anything before? Grant them, Lord, to think hard about what they are saying, and to find that never cannot be said where there is no time. To say that he never made anything — what is that but to say that he made it in no time? Let them see, then, that there can be no time without a created world, and let them stop talking that empty talk. Let them too be stretched toward the things that are before; let them understand that you are before all times, the eternal Creator of all times, and that no times are coeternal with you, and no creature either, even if there is some creature before all times.

Lord my God, what a depth is this hidden recess of your mysteries — and how far from it the consequences of my sins have flung me! Heal my eyes, that I may share in the joy of your light. Surely, if there is a mind so richly gifted with knowledge and foreknowledge that it knows all things past and to come as well as I know one familiar psalm, that mind is wonderful past all telling, dreadful and astonishing — since nothing of the past, nothing of the ages to come, is any more hidden from it than, when I sang that psalm, it was hidden from me what and how much of it had passed away from the start, and what and how much remained until the end. But far be it that you, the Creator of the universe, the Creator of souls and bodies — far be it that you should know all things past and to come in such a way as that. Far, far more wonderfully, far more mysteriously, do you know them. For with the man who sings a song he knows, or hears a familiar one, his feelings vary, and his senses are divided, by his expecting the words to come and remembering the words gone by; but nothing of the sort happens to you, unchangeably eternal, the truly eternal Creator of minds. And so, just as in the Beginning you knew heaven and earth without any change in your knowing, so in the Beginning you made heaven and earth without any pulling-apart of your action. Let whoever understands this confess to you; and whoever does not understand it, let him confess to you too. Oh, how high you are — and yet the humble in heart are your dwelling place; for you lift up those who are bowed down, and they do not fall, whose lifting-up is you.
books.title: Time and Eternity

books.label: Book XII
paragraphs: O Lord, my heart is busy over the words of your holy Scripture, here in the poverty of my life. And this is why, most of the time, the poverty of human understanding runs on in so many words: because asking has more to say than finding, and the knocking lasts longer than the opening, and the hand that knocks has more work to do than the hand that receives. Yet we hold your promise; who shall cancel it? If God is for us, who can be against us? Ask, and you shall be given; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. These are your own promises; and who could fear to be cheated, when the Truth is the one who promises?

From the lowliness of my tongue I confess to your highness that you made heaven and earth — this heaven I see, and this earth I tread on, the earth I carry about in my own body: you made it. But where, O Lord, is that heaven of heavens we hear of in the words of the Psalm, the heaven of heavens is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men? Where is that heaven we cannot see, the one to which everything we can see is only earth? For this whole bodily world is not present everywhere at once; it has received its measure of beauty even down here in these lower regions, of which the very lowest is this earth of ours. But set beside that heaven of heavens, even the sky over our earth is only earth; and it is not absurd to call both of these great bodies earth, compared with that unknown heaven which is the Lord's and not the sons' of men.

Now this earth was invisible and unformed, and there was some unfathomable depth, an abyss with no light upon it, because it had no shape. That is why you commanded it to be written that darkness was upon the face of the deep. And what is darkness but the absence of light? For had there been light, where would it have been but up over everything, shining down? Where light was not, then, what was the presence of darkness but the absence of light — just as where there is no sound, there is silence, and to have silence in a place is simply to have no sound in it? Have you not taught this, O Lord, to the soul that confesses to you? Have you not taught me, Lord, that before you formed and shaped this formless matter, there was nothing — no color, no figure, no body, no spirit? And yet not altogether nothing: there was a certain formlessness, without any beauty at all.

What should it be called, then, so that it could be conveyed in some measure even to slower minds, except by some ordinary word? And among all the parts of the world, what comes nearer to sheer formlessness than earth and the deep? Lying at the lowest level, they are less beautiful than the higher parts, which are all transparent and shining. So why may I not take it that the formlessness of matter — which you had made without beauty, that you might make this beautiful world out of it — was fittingly hinted to us under the name of earth invisible and unformed?

So when thought goes looking for what the senses might lay hold of under this name, and says to itself, It is no intelligible form, like life or justice, since it is the stuff of bodies; and it is no object of the senses either, since, being invisible and unformed, there was in it nothing to see or to feel — while a man's thought says this to itself, it can only try either to know it by being ignorant of it, or to be ignorant of it by knowing it.

But, Lord, if I were to confess to you with my tongue and my pen the whole of whatever you have taught me about that matter — I, who used to hear the very name before I understood it, when those who did not understand it told me of it, and so I pictured it as having countless different forms, and therefore did not picture it at all, my mind tossing up foul and horrible shapes, all out of order, but still shapes; and I called it formless not because it lacked all form, but because it had the sort my mind would turn away from if it met them, as strange and jarring, the sort that would trouble human frailty. And even what I did picture was formless not because it was stripped of every form, but only by comparison with more beautiful forms. True reason kept persuading me that I must strip off every last remnant of form whatsoever, if I wanted to conceive matter utterly without form — and I could not. Sooner could I judge that a thing deprived of all form simply did not exist, than conceive something halfway between form and nothing, neither formed nor nothing, a formless almost-nothing. So my mind gave up questioning my own spirit about it, for my spirit was filled with the images of formed bodies, shifting and varying them as it pleased; and I turned instead to bodies themselves and looked more deeply into their changeableness, by which they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. And this very passing from one form to another I suspected took place through some formless state, and not through sheer nothing — though I longed to know this, not merely to suspect it. If, then, my voice and my pen were to confess to you the whole of every knot you untied for me in this question, what reader could hold on to take it all in? And yet my heart will not for that reason stop giving you honor and a song of praise for the things it cannot put into words. For the changeableness of changeable things is itself capable of taking on all the forms into which changeable things are changed. And this changeableness — what is it? Is it soul? Is it body? Is it some likeness of soul or body? If one could say a nothing-something, an is-and-is-not, I would say it was this; and yet in some way it already was, since it was capable of receiving these visible, composite shapes.

But where did it get even this much of being, except from you, from whom all things have being insofar as they are at all? Only the more unlike you a thing is, the further from you — and not by any distance of place. So you, Lord, who are not one thing here and another thing there, but the Selfsame, the Selfsame, the Selfsame, Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty — in the Beginning, which is from you, in your Wisdom, which was born of your own substance, you made something, and made it out of nothing. For you made heaven and earth, but not out of yourself; otherwise they would have been equal to your only-begotten Son, and so to you as well, and it could never be right that anything should be equal to you which was not from you. And there was nothing else besides you out of which you might make them, O God, one Trinity and threefold Unity; and so out of nothing you made heaven and earth, a great thing and a small thing, for you are almighty and good, able to make all things good — the great heaven and the little earth alike. You were, and nothing else was, out of which you made heaven and earth: two kinds of thing, one near to you, the other near to nothing; one with you alone above it, the other with nothing below it.

But that heaven of heavens was for yourself, O Lord. The earth, though — the earth you gave to the sons of men to be seen and touched — was not yet the earth we now see and touch. For it was invisible and unformed, and there was a deep over which there was no light; or rather, darkness was over the deep, that is, more than merely in the deep. For the deep of waters we now see has, even in its depths, a light suited to its nature, perceived in some degree by the fish and the creeping things at the bottom of it. But that whole deep was almost nothing, since up to then it was wholly without form; and yet there was already that which could be formed. For you, Lord, made the world out of formless matter, and that matter you made out of nothing — next to nothing — to make from it the great things we sons of men marvel at. For this bodily heaven is a wonder indeed, this firmament between water and water which, on the second day, after the making of light, you said, Let it be made, and it was made. This firmament you called heaven — the heaven of this earth and sea, which you made on the third day by giving a visible shape to the formless matter you had made before any day. For you had already made a heaven before all days, but that was the heaven of this heaven; because In the beginning you had made heaven and earth. But this earth that you made was formless matter, since it was invisible and unformed and darkness was upon the deep; and out of this invisible and unformed earth, out of this formlessness, this almost-nothing, you were to make all these things of which this changing world consists — though it has no firm standing, for its very changeableness shows itself in this, that times can be marked and counted in it. For times are made by the alterations of things, as the shapes are varied and turned, whose underlying matter is that invisible earth.

And so the Spirit, the teacher of your servant, when it tells how In the Beginning you created heaven and earth, says nothing of times, nothing of days. For truly that heaven of heavens which you created in the Beginning is some intelligent creature, which, though in no way coeternal with you, the Trinity, still has a share in your eternity, and through the sweetness of that most happy contemplation of you holds its own changeableness firmly in check; and, never having fallen since it was first made, clinging close to you, it stands beyond all the rolling change of times. And neither is that very formlessness of the earth — invisible and unformed — reckoned among the days. For where there is no shape and no order, nothing comes and nothing goes; and where this is so, there plainly are no days, no turning round of stretches of time.

O let the Light, the Truth, the Light of my heart, and not my own darkness, speak to me. I slipped down into that darkness and was darkened; but even from there, even from there I loved you. I went astray, and remembered you. I heard your voice behind me, calling me to return, and I scarcely heard it through the uproar of the enemies of peace. And now, look, I am coming back, gasping and panting after your fountain. Let no one keep me from it. From this I will drink, and so I will live. Let me not be my own life; out of myself I lived badly, I was death to myself; in you I come alive again. Speak to me, talk with me. I have believed your Books, and their words are full of mystery.

Already, Lord, you have told me with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you are eternal, you who alone have immortality; since you cannot be changed in shape or in motion, and your will is not altered by the passing of time — for no will that varies is immortal. This is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings. You have told me also with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that you have made all natures and all substances which are not what you yourself are, and yet are; and that the only thing not from you is what has no being at all, and the swerving of the will away from you, who are, toward something that is to a lesser degree — for that swerving is transgression and sin. And no one's sin either harms you or disturbs the order of your rule, first or last. This too is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings.

You have told me also with a strong voice, in my inner ear, that not even that creature is coeternal with you whose whole happiness is you alone, and which, drinking its nourishment from you with a most steadfast purity, nowhere and at no time lets its natural changeableness break out; for, with you ever present to it, to whom it holds with its whole love, it has no future to wait for and carries nothing it remembers off into the past, and so it is neither altered by any change nor pulled apart into times. O blessed creature — if such there is — for clinging to your blessedness; blessed in you, its eternal dweller and its light! I can find no better name for that heaven of heavens which is the Lord's than your house — the house that contemplates your delight without ever lapsing into a turning-away toward something else; one pure mind, knit together in the most perfect oneness by the settled peace of holy spirits, the citizens of your city in the heavenly places, far above these heavenly places that we can see.

By this the soul whose pilgrimage has carried it long and far away may understand — if by now it thirsts for you, if by now its tears have become its bread while day after day they say to it, Where is your God? — if by now it asks one thing of you and longs for it, that it may dwell in your house all the days of its life. And what is its life but you? And what are your days but your eternity, your years that do not fail, because you are always the same? By this, then, the soul that is able may understand how far above all times you are, eternal; seeing that your house, which has never gone off into any far country, though it is not coeternal with you, yet by clinging to you ceaselessly and without failing, suffers no changeableness of times. This is clear to me in your sight; let it be made clearer and clearer to me, I beg you, and in that unveiling let me rest soberly under your wings.

There is, I confess, some formlessness or other in these changes of the lowest and last of creatures. And who shall tell me — unless it be some empty-hearted man, who wanders and tosses himself up and down among his own fancies — who but such a one would tell me that, if every shape were so worn and consumed away that only that formlessness remained, through which a thing was changed and turned from one shape to another, this could still display the turning of times? It plainly could not, because without a variety of motions there are no times, and there is no variety where there is no shape.

Having considered these things, as much as you give me to, O my God, as much as you stir me up to knock, and as much as you open to me when I knock, I find two things you have made that are not within the reach of time, though neither is coeternal with you. One is so formed that, without any break in its contemplation, without any interval of change — changeable, yet not changed — it fully enjoys your eternity and your unchangeableness. The other was so formless that it had nothing in it that could be changed from one form to another, neither in motion nor in rest, so as to be subject to time. But you did not leave this one formless, for before any day, in the Beginning, you created Heaven and Earth — the two things I have been speaking of. But the Earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep. In these words the formlessness is conveyed to us — so that minds unable to conceive an utter absence of all form, short of arriving at nothing, may be led on by degrees — the formlessness out of which another Heaven was to be made, together with a visible and well-formed earth, and the waters set in their different orders, and whatever else is recorded to have been made, not without days, in the forming of the world; things of such a nature that the successive changes of times can take place in them, since they are subject to their appointed alterations of motion and of form.

This, then, is what I take it to mean, O my God, when I hear your Scripture say, In the beginning God made Heaven and Earth, and the Earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep — and it names no day on which you made them. This is what I take it to mean: that because of the Heaven of heavens, that intelligible Heaven whose minds know all at once — not in part, not darkly, not through a glass, but as a whole, openly, face to face; not this thing now and that thing next, but, as I said, all at once, with no succession of times — and because of the earth invisible and unformed, which likewise has no succession of times, for succession is what gives us this thing now and that thing next, and where there is no form there is no marking off of one thing from another — because of these two, a thing first formed and a thing first formless, the one heaven but the Heaven of heaven, the other earth but the earth invisible and unformed, because of these two, your Scripture said, without mentioning days, In the Beginning God created Heaven and Earth. For at once it added which earth it meant; and since the Firmament is recorded as made on the second day and called Heaven, this tells us which Heaven it had spoken of before, without mention of days.

What a marvelous depth there is in your words! Their surface, look, lies open before us, inviting the little ones; and yet, what a marvelous depth, O my God, a marvelous depth! It strikes awe to look into it — the awe of honor, the trembling of love. Its enemies I hate fiercely; oh that you would slay them with your two-edged sword, that they might be its enemies no longer! For this is how I love to have them slain to themselves: that they may live to you. But look, there are others who do not find fault with the book of Genesis but praise it, and yet they say: The Spirit of God, who wrote these things through his servant Moses, did not mean those words to be understood as you say, but otherwise, as we say. To them, with you as judge over us all, my God, this is how I answer.

Will you call it false, what Truth tells me with a strong voice in my inner ear about the eternity of the Creator — that his substance is in no way changed by time, and his will is not separate from his substance? Therefore he does not will one thing now and another thing next, but once, and all at once, and forever, he wills everything that he wills; not again and again, not now this and now that, nor does he will afterward what before he did not, nor stop willing what before he willed; for a will like that is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal — but our God is eternal. And again, what Truth tells me in my inner ear: that the looking-forward to things to come becomes the seeing of them when they are here, and this same seeing becomes memory when they are past; and all thought that varies in this way is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal — but our God is eternal. These things I gather and put together, and I find that my God, the eternal God, did not make any creature by some new act of will, nor does his knowledge take in anything passing. What will you say, then, you who contradict me? Are these things false? No, they say. What then? Is it false, that every nature already formed, and every matter capable of form, has its being only from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is? No, we do not deny that either, they say. What then? Do you deny that there is a certain lofty creature which clings with so chaste a love to the true and truly eternal God that, though not coeternal with him, it is never torn away from him, never dissolved into the variety and changing of times, but rests in the most true contemplation of him alone? For you, O God, show yourself and are enough for the one who loves you as much as you command; and so he does not turn away from you, nor toward himself. This is the house of God, not made of earthly stuff, nor of any heavenly bulk of body, but spiritual, and a sharer in your eternity, because it is forever without lapse. For you have made it firm forever and ever; you have given it a law it shall not overstep. And yet it is not coeternal with you, O God, because it is not without a beginning — for it was made.

For although we find no time before it, since wisdom was created before all things — not that Wisdom which is altogether equal and coeternal with you, our God, its Father, by whom all things were made, in whom, as the Beginning, you made heaven and earth, but a created wisdom, that is, the intelligent nature which becomes light by contemplating the Light. For this, though created, is also called wisdom. But the difference between the Light that gives light and the light that receives it is the same as the difference between the Wisdom that creates and the wisdom that is created, as between the Righteousness that justifies and the righteousness made by justification. For we too are called your righteousness, since one of your servants says, That we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Since, then, a certain created wisdom was created before all things — the rational and intelligent mind of that chaste city of yours, our mother who is above and is free and eternal in the heavens (in what heavens, if not in those that praise you, the Heaven of heavens? for this also is the Heaven of heavens that belongs to the Lord) — though we find no time before it, because what was created before all things comes before time's own creatures too, yet the Eternity of the Creator himself is before it, the Creator from whom, being made, it took its beginning — not a beginning in time, for time itself was not yet, but the beginning of its being created.

And so it is from you, our God, in such a way as to be altogether other than you, and not the Selfsame. For although we find no time before it, nor even in it, since it is fit ever to behold your face and is never drawn away from it, and so is never varied by any change, yet there is in it a liability to change, by which it would grow dark and cold, were it not that, clinging to you with a strong love like a perpetual noon, it shines and glows from you. O house full of light, full of delight! I have loved your beauty, and the place where the glory of my Lord dwells, your builder and possessor. Let my wandering sigh after you; and I say to him who made you, let him take possession of me too in you, since he made me as well. I have gone astray like a lost sheep; yet upon the shoulders of my Shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried back to you.

What do you say to me, you who contradict me, you to whom I was speaking — you who do, after all, believe Moses to have been the holy servant of God, and his books the oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is not this house of God — not coeternal with God, indeed, but in its own measure eternal in the heavens — a place where you look in vain for changes of times, because you will not find them? For that to which it is always good to cling fast to God rises above all stretching-out and all the revolving cycles of time. It is, they say. Then what of all that my heart cried aloud to my God, when inwardly it heard the voice of his praise — what part of it do you call false? Is it that the matter was without form, in which, because there was no form, there was no order; and where there was no order, there could be no turning of times — and yet this almost-nothing, since it was not altogether nothing, was certainly from him, from whom is whatever is, in whatever degree it is? This too, they say, we do not deny.

With these men I will now talk a little while in your presence, O my God — these men who grant that all these things are true, which your Truth whispers to my soul. For those who deny them, let them bark and deafen themselves as much as they please; I will try to coax them into quiet and to open in them a way for your word. But if they refuse and turn me away, then I beg you, my God, do not be silent to me. Speak truly in my heart, for only you speak so; and I will leave them outside, blowing on the dust and raising it up into their own eyes, and I will go into my room and there sing a song of love to you, groaning with groans beyond words on my pilgrimage, remembering Jerusalem with my heart stretched up toward it — Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother, and you who rule over it, the Light-giver, the Father, the Guardian, the Husband, the pure and strong delight, the solid joy, and all good things beyond speech, all of them at once, because you are the one sovereign and true Good. And I will not be turned aside until you gather all of me, out of this scattered and disordered state, into the peace of that mother most dear, where the first-fruits of my spirit already are, and from which I am made sure of these things, and you shape me and make me firm forever, O my God, my Mercy. But to those who do not call all these truths false, who honor your holy Scripture set forth by holy Moses, placing it, as we do, at the very summit of authority to be followed, and yet contradict me on some point, I answer this: be yourself the judge, O our God, between my confessions and these men's contradictions.

For they say: Even if these things are true, still Moses did not have those two in mind when, by revelation of the Spirit, he said, In the beginning God created heaven and earth. He did not mean, under the name of heaven, that spiritual or intelligible creature which always beholds the face of God; nor, under the name of earth, that formless matter. What then? That man of God, they say, meant what we say; this is what he declared by those words. What is that? By the name of heaven and earth, they say, he first meant to signify, all together and in brief, this whole visible world, so that afterward, by listing the several days, he might lay out in detail, piece by piece, all those things which it pleased the Holy Spirit to set forth in this way. For that rough and earthbound people he spoke to was such that he judged them fit to be told only of those works of God that could be seen. They do agree, however, that under the words earth invisible and unformed, and that dark deep — out of which, it is afterward shown, all these visible things we know were made and set in order during those days — one may, not unfittingly, understand this formless first matter.

What now if someone else should say that this same formlessness and confusion of matter was first set down under the name of heaven and earth for this reason: that out of it was made this visible world, with all the natures that most plainly appear in it, the world that is so often itself called by the name heaven and earth, once it is made and finished? Or what if another should say that the invisible and the visible nature are not inaptly called heaven and earth, and so the whole creation, which God made in his Wisdom — that is, in the Beginning — was gathered up under those two words; but since all things are made not out of the substance of God but out of nothing, because they are not the same as God is, and there is a changeable nature in them all, whether they abide, as the eternal house of God does, or are changed, as the soul and body of a man are — that therefore the common matter of all things visible and invisible, still unformed but capable of form, out of which both heaven and earth were to be made (that is, the invisible and the visible creation once formed), was named by the very same names given to the earth invisible and unformed and to the darkness upon the deep, but with this difference: that by the earth invisible and unformed is meant bodily matter before it took on any form, and by the darkness upon the deep, spiritual matter before any check was put on its unbounded fluidity, before it received any light from Wisdom?

And there is still room for a man to say, if he likes, that the already finished and formed natures, visible and invisible, are not what is meant under the name of heaven and earth when we read, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, but rather that the still-unformed first stage of things, the stuff fit to take on form and making, was called by these names, because in it were held together, all confused, not yet sorted out by their qualities and forms, all those things which, now arranged in order, are called Heaven and Earth — the one the spiritual, the other the bodily creation.

Having heard and weighed all this, I have no wish to fight about words, which is good for nothing but the ruin of those who listen. The law, though, is good for building up, if a man uses it lawfully, for its end is charity, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned. And our Master knew well on which two commandments he hung all the Law and the Prophets. So what does it matter to me, O my God, light of my eyes in their secret place, while I confess these things in earnest — since many things, all of them true, may be understood under these words — what, I say, does it harm me if I think the writer meant one thing where another thinks he meant something else? All of us who read are truly trying to track down and grasp the meaning of the one we read; and since we believe he spoke the truth, we dare not imagine him to have said anything we ourselves know or believe to be false. So while each one is straining to understand in the holy Scriptures the very thing the writer understood, what harm is there if a man understands something that you, the light of all truth-speaking minds, show him to be true — even if the one he reads did not understand this particular truth, seeing that he too understood a truth, though not this truth?

For it is true, O Lord, that you made heaven and earth; and true that the Beginning is your Wisdom, in which you made all things; and true again that this visible world has for its greater parts the heaven and the earth, which in two words take in all made and created natures. And true that whatever is changeable gives us to understand a certain lack of form, by which it takes on a form, or is changed, or turned. And true that whatever clings to the unchangeable Form in such a way that, though it could be changed, it is never changed, is subject to no times. True that the formlessness which is almost nothing cannot be subject to the change of times. True that the thing a thing is made from may, by a certain way of speaking, be called by the name of the thing made from it; and so that formlessness, out of which heaven and earth were made, might be called heaven and earth. True that of all things having form, none is nearer to having no form than the earth and the deep. True that not only every created and formed thing, but whatever is even capable of being created and formed, you made, you from whom are all things. And true that whatever is formed out of what had no form was unformed before it was formed.

Out of these truths, which they do not doubt whose inner eye you have enabled to see such things, and who unshakably believe your servant Moses spoke in the Spirit of truth — out of all of these, one man takes this one, who says, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the intelligible and the sensible, that is, the spiritual and the bodily creation. Another takes this: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the whole bulk of this bodily world, with all the plain and familiar creatures it holds. Another: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God made the formless matter of the spiritual and bodily creatures. Another: In the Beginning God created heaven and earth, meaning, in his Word coeternal with himself God created the formless matter of the bodily creation, in which heaven and earth still lay confused together, the same heaven and earth that, now sorted out and formed, we see today in the bulk of this world. And another, who says: In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, meaning, in the very beginning of his creating and working God made that formless matter, holding confusedly within itself both heaven and earth, out of which, now that they are formed, they stand out and are plain to see, with all that is in them.

And as for the understanding of the words that follow, out of all those truths one man chooses for himself this one, who says, But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep, meaning that the bodily thing God made was as yet a formless matter of bodily things, without order, without light. Another says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep, meaning that this whole, called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which the bodily heaven and the bodily earth were to be made, with all the things in them that our bodily senses know. Another says it meaning that this whole, called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, out of which were to be made both that intelligible heaven, elsewhere called the Heaven of heavens, and the earth, that is, the whole bodily nature, under which name this bodily sky too is taken in — in a word, out of which every visible and invisible creature was to be created. Another says it meaning that Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth, but that the formlessness already existed, which he called the earth invisible and unformed, and darkness upon the deep, of which it had been said just before that God made heaven and earth, namely the spiritual and bodily creation. And another says it meaning that there already was a certain formless matter, of which Scripture had said before that God made heaven and earth, namely the whole bodily bulk of the world, split into two great parts, the upper and the lower, with all the common and familiar creatures in them.

Now suppose someone should try to argue against these last two opinions like this: If you will not allow that this formlessness of matter seems to be called by the name of heaven and earth, then there was something God had not made, out of which to make heaven and earth; for Scripture has not told us that God made this matter, unless we take it to be signified by the name of heaven and earth, or of earth alone, where it is said, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth — so that in what follows, and the earth was invisible and unformed (even granting that it pleased him to call the formless matter by this name), we are to understand no other matter than the one God made, of which it was written just above, God made heaven and earth. To this the defenders of either of those last two opinions, when they hear it, will answer: We do not at all deny that this formless matter was created by God, the God from whom are all things, very good; for just as we hold that to be a greater good which is created and formed, so we confess that to be a lesser good which is only made capable of creation and form — yet still good. But we say that Scripture has not set down that God made this formlessness, just as it has not set down many other things, such as the Cherubim and Seraphim, and those the Apostle names so distinctly, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers — all of which, plainly, God made. Or if in the words, He made heaven and earth, everything is taken in, then what shall we say of the waters, over which the Spirit of God moved? If they are included in the word earth, how then can formless matter be meant by the name of earth, when we see the waters so beautiful? Or if it is so taken, why then is it written that out of the same formlessness the firmament was made and called heaven, while it is not written that the waters were made? For the waters do not remain formless and invisible — we behold them flowing in so lovely a way. But if they received that beauty when God said, Let the waters under the firmament be gathered together, so that the gathering is itself their forming, what shall be said of those waters above the firmament? For if they were formless they would not have been worthy of so honorable a seat, and it is not written by what word they were formed. So if Genesis is silent about God's making of something which God nonetheless did make, as neither sound faith nor sound understanding doubts — and no sober teaching would dare to call these waters coeternal with God, just because we find them named in the book of Genesis while we do not find when they were created — then why, since truth teaches us, should we not understand that the formless matter, which this Scripture calls the earth invisible and unformed and the dark deep, was created by God out of nothing, and so is not coeternal with him, even though this history has left out telling when it was created?

Having heard and grasped these things, as far as my small capacity allows — which I confess to you, O Lord, you who know it — I see that two sorts of disagreement may arise when something is related in words by truthful reporters: one about the truth of the things themselves, the other about the meaning of the one who reports them. For we ask one question about the making of the creation, what is true; and another about what Moses, that excellent minister of your faith, would have his reader and hearer understand by those words. As for the first sort, away with all those who imagine they know as true what is in fact false; and as for the second, away with all those too who imagine Moses wrote things that are false. But let me be joined, O Lord, in you, with these others, and let me delight myself in you together with those who feed on your truth in the broad room of charity; and let us draw near together to the words of your book and seek in them your meaning through the meaning of your servant, by whose pen you have dealt them out to us.

But which of us, among all those many truths that come to mind in those words as they are differently understood, can so single out that one meaning as to declare, This is what Moses thought, this is what he meant to be understood in that history, with the same confidence he would say, This is true, whether Moses thought it or not? For look, O my God, I your servant, who in this book have vowed a sacrifice of confession to you, and pray that by your mercy I may pay my vows to you — can I, with the same confidence with which I declare that in your unchangeable Word you made all things visible and invisible, also declare that Moses meant nothing other than this when he wrote, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth? No. Because I do not see it in his mind, that he was thinking of this when he wrote these things, as I do see it to be certain in your truth. For he might have had his thoughts on God's first act of creating when he said In the beginning; and by heaven and earth, here, he might have meant no formed and finished nature, whether spiritual or bodily, but both of them just begun and still formless. For I see that whichever of the two had been said, it could have been truly said; but which of the two he had in mind when he wrote these words, I do not so plainly see. And yet, whether it was one of these, or some other sense I have not mentioned here, that so great a man saw in his mind when he uttered these words, I do not doubt that he saw it truly and put it aptly.

Let no one badger me, then, by saying, Moses did not think as you say, but as I say. For if he were to ask me, How do you know that Moses thought what you draw out of his words? I ought to take it in good part, and would answer perhaps as I have above, or more fully if he kept pressing. But when he says, Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say — and yet does not deny that what each of us says may both be true — then, O my God, life of the poor, in whose bosom there is no contradiction, pour down a softening dew into my heart, that I may bear patiently with those who say this to me. They say it not because they are godly men and have seen in the heart of your servant what they claim, but because they are proud; they do not know Moses' meaning, but love their own — not because it is true, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would love another true opinion just as much, the way I love what they say when they say something true, not because it is theirs but because it is true, and on that very account no longer theirs, because it is true. But because they insist Moses meant not what I say but what they say, this I do not like, do not love; for even were it so, that rashness of theirs comes not from knowledge but from sheer boldness, and not insight but vanity is its parent. And so, O Lord, your judgments are to be feared, since your truth is not mine, nor his, nor anyone's, but belongs to us all, whom you call openly to share in it, warning us terribly not to treat it as our own private property, or we will be cut off from it. For whoever lays claim to as his own what you set before all to enjoy, and wants for himself alone what belongs to all, is driven out of what is held in common into what is his own — that is, out of truth into a lie. For whoever speaks a lie speaks from what is his own.

Listen, O God, best of judges, Truth itself, listen to what I say to this man who contradicts me — listen, for I speak before you and before my brothers, who use your law lawfully, to the end of charity. Listen and look, if it please you, at what I say to him. For this is the brotherly and peaceful word I give him back: If we both see that what you say is true, and both see that what I say is true, where, I ask you, do we see it? Surely not I in you, nor you in me, but both of us in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our minds. Since, then, we are not quarreling over the very light of the Lord our God, why do we quarrel over the thoughts of our neighbor, which we cannot see as the unchangeable Truth is seen? For even if Moses himself appeared to us and said, This is what I meant, we would not see it, but would only believe it.
