Let us not, then, be puffed up one against another beyond what is written; let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. And with these two precepts of charity in view, unless we believe that Moses meant whatever in those books he did mean, we shall make God a liar, by imagining our fellow servant's mind to be other than what God has taught us. See, then, how foolish it is, amid such a wealth of perfectly true meanings as can be drawn out of those words, to assert rashly which of them Moses chiefly meant, and with ruinous quarrels to wound charity itself — the very thing for whose sake he said everything we are trying to expound.

And yet I, O my God — you who lift up my lowliness and are the rest of my labor, you who hear my confessions and forgive my sins — since you command me to love my neighbor as myself, I cannot believe that you gave a smaller gift to Moses, your faithful servant, than I would have wished or longed for you to give me, had I been born in his time and had you set me in that office, that through the service of my heart and tongue those books might be handed down which were for so long after to do good to all nations, and from such a height of authority were to overtop all the sayings of false and proud teachings. I should truly have wished, had I then been Moses — for we all come from the same lump, and what is man, unless you are mindful of him? — I would then, had I been what he was, and been charged by you to write the book of Genesis, have wished for such power of expression and such a way of writing to be given me that neither those who cannot yet understand how God creates would reject the words as beyond their reach, nor those who could understand would find any true opinion they had reached by their own thought passed over in those few words of your servant; and that if another man, by the light of truth, had found yet another meaning, that too should not fail to be found in those same words.

For just as a spring within a narrow space is more abundant, and feeds streams over wider ground than any one of the streams that flows, after a long way, from that same spring, so the account of that steward of yours, meant to benefit many who would discourse upon it, overflows out of a small measure of language into streams of the clearest truth, from which each one may draw out for himself such truth as he can on these matters — one this truth, another that — by longer roundabout ways of speaking. For some, when they read or hear these words, imagine that God, like a man or some mass endowed with boundless power, by some new and sudden decision made heaven and earth outside himself, as it were at a certain distance, two great bodies above and below, in which all things were to be contained. And when they hear, God said, Let it be made, and it was made, they imagine words that began and ended, sounding in time and passing away, after whose passing the thing came into being that had been commanded to be — and whatever else of this kind their acquaintance with the material world would suggest. In such people, still little ones and earthbound, while their weakness is carried along by this humble manner of speech as in a mother's lap, their faith is wholesomely built up, so that they hold it sure that God made all the natures their eyes behold around them in such marvelous variety. But if any of them, scorning these words as too simple, should in proud weakness stretch himself out beyond the sheltering nest, then — alas — he will fall miserably. Have pity, O Lord God, lest those who pass by trample the unfledged bird, and send your angel to put it back in the nest, that it may live until it can fly.

But there are others to whom these words are no longer a nest but a deep, shady orchard; they see the fruit hidden in it, fly joyously around, and with cheerful cries seek it out and pick it. For when they read or hear these words, they see that all times past and to come are surpassed by your eternal and steadfast abiding, and that even so there is no creature formed in time that is not of your making. They see that your will, because it is the very thing you are, made all things by no change of will, by no will that before was not; and that these things were made not out of yourself, in your own likeness, which is the form of all things, but out of nothing, a formless unlikeness, to be formed by your likeness — returning, each to your Unity, according to the measure appointed to it, as far as is granted to each thing in its kind — and all to be made very good, whether they remain close around you or, removed by degrees in time and place, make or undergo the beautiful changes of the universe. These things they see, and they rejoice, in the small measure they can here, in the light of your truth.

Another bends his mind on what is said, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth, and sees in the Beginning Wisdom, because it also speaks to us. Another likewise bends his mind on the same words, and by Beginning understands the mere starting of things created — In the beginning he made, as if it were said, He at first made. And among those who understand In the Beginning to mean, In your Wisdom you made heaven and earth, one believes that the matter out of which heaven and earth were to be made is what is here called heaven and earth; another, natures already formed and distinct; another, one formed nature, and that a spiritual one, under the name Heaven, and the other formless, a bodily matter, under the name Earth. And those who by the names heaven and earth understand matter still formless, out of which heaven and earth were to be formed, do not all understand it in one way either: one means the matter out of which both the intelligible and the sensible creation were to be perfected, another only the matter out of which this sensible bodily mass was to be made, holding in its vast bosom these visible and ordinary natures. Nor do those who believe the creatures already ordered and arranged are here called heaven and earth understand it the same: one means both the invisible and the visible, another only the visible, in which we behold this bright sky and this dark earth, with the things they contain.

But the one who understands In the Beginning he made no otherwise than as if it were said, At first he made, can only truly understand heaven and earth as the matter of heaven and earth, that is, of the whole intelligible and bodily creation. For if he wished to understand by it the universe already formed, it could rightly be asked of him, If God made this first, what did he make afterward? And after the universe he will find nothing; whereupon, against his will, he must hear another question: How did God make this first, if nothing came after? But when he says, God made matter first formless, then formed, there is no absurdity, provided he is able to tell apart what comes before by eternity, what by time, what by choice, and what in origin. By eternity, as God is before all things; by time, as the flower before the fruit; by choice, as the fruit before the flower; by origin, as the sound before the tune. Of these four, the first and the last are understood only with great difficulty, the two middle ones easily. For it is a rare and lofty sight, O Lord, to behold your Eternity, unchangeably making things changeable, and so being before them. And who, again, is sharp-sighted enough to discern without great labor how the sound is therefore before the tune — because a tune is a formed sound, and a thing not formed can exist, whereas a thing that does not exist cannot be formed? Just so the matter is before the thing made from it: not because it makes that thing, since rather it is itself made; nor before it by any interval of time. For we do not first utter formless sounds without singing, and afterward shape and fit them into the form of a chant, as wood or silver out of which a chest or a vessel is made. For such materials do precede in time the forms of the things made from them; but in singing it is not so, for when it is sung, its sound is heard at once: there is not first a formless sound, afterward formed into a chant. For every sound, as soon as it is made, passes away, and you can find nothing to call back and by art to compose. So the chant is held together in its sound, which sound is its matter. And this is indeed formed, that it may be a tune; and therefore, as I said, the matter of the sound is before the form of the tune — not before it by any power to make it, for a sound is in no way the maker of the tune, but is something bodily, put under the soul that sings, out of which to make a tune; nor first in time, for it is given out together with the tune; nor first in choice, for a sound is no better than a tune, since a tune is not merely a sound but a beautiful sound. But it is first in origin, because a tune does not receive form in order to become a sound, but a sound receives form in order to become a tune. By this example let the one who is able understand how the matter of things was first made and called heaven and earth, because heaven and earth were made from it — and yet it was not made first in time, since it is the forms of things that give rise to time, while that matter was without form, and only now, in time, is an object of the senses together with its form. And yet nothing can be told of that matter except as though it came earlier in time, while in worth it comes last, because formed things are higher than things without form; and it is preceded by the Eternity of the Creator, so that out of nothing there might be something from which something could be made.

In this variety of true opinions, let Truth herself bring forth concord; and let our God have mercy on us, that we may use the law lawfully, to its end, the pure charity of the commandment. By this, if anyone asks me, Which of these was the meaning of your servant Moses? — this would not be the language of my Confessions, if I did not confess to you, I do not know. And yet I know that those senses are true, except for the earthbound ones, of which I have said what seemed necessary. And even those hopeful little ones who think in that earthbound way have this benefit, that the words of your Book do not frighten them, since they utter high things in a lowly way, a rich meaning in few words. And all of us who, I confess, see and speak the truth set down in those words — let us love one another, and together love you, our God, the fountain of truth, if we are truly thirsting for it and not for empty things. And let us so honor this servant of yours, the dispenser of this Scripture, full of your Spirit, as to believe that, when by your revelation he wrote these things, he had in view whichever meaning among them most excels both for light of truth and for richness of profit.

So when one man says, Moses meant as I do, and another, No, but as I do, I think I speak more reverently when I say, Why not as both, if both are true? And if there is a third, or a fourth, indeed if anyone sees yet another truth in those words, why may he not be believed to have seen all of them — he through whom the one God shaped the holy Scriptures to fit the understandings of many, who would see in them things true but different? For I, at least — and I say it from my heart without fear — were I to write anything to have the highest authority, I would rather write so that whatever truth anyone could grasp on these matters might be conveyed by my words, than set down one meaning of my own so plainly as to shut out the rest, which, not being false, could give me no offense. I will not, then, O my God, be so rash as not to believe that you granted as much to that great man. He, beyond doubt, when he wrote those words, perceived and had in mind whatever truth we have been able to find in them, and whatever we have not been able to find, and are not yet able to, but which may still be found in them.

Lastly, O Lord, you who are God and not flesh and blood — if a man saw less, could anything be hidden from your good Spirit, who shall lead me into the land of uprightness, anything that you yourself were about to reveal, by those very words, to readers in times to come, even though the one through whom they were spoken perhaps had in mind, among many true meanings, only some single one? And if that is how it is, then let the one he had in mind be the highest of all. But to us, O Lord, either reveal that same meaning, or any other true one that pleases you, so that whether you uncover to us the same as to your servant, or some other by occasion of those words, you may still feed us, and no error deceive us. Look, O Lord my God, how much we have written on a few words — how much, I beg you! What strength of ours, what ages, would be enough for all your books at this rate? Let me, then, confess to you in these things more briefly, and choose some one true, certain, and good sense that you shall inspire, even where many present themselves, where many may; this being the law of my confession: that if I should say what your minister meant, that is right and best, and that is what I should strive for; and if I should not reach it, then I should still say what your Truth willed to tell me by his words — your Truth, which told him too what it willed.
